utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is IT-05-87-T, the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. For the commencement of the trial you will see we are joined by Judge Nosworthy, as I intimated on Friday, who is the Reserve Judge in this trial. I now invite the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis, to make his opening statement. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. During my presentation this morning, Your Honour, we will be showing you some visuals, and I understand it may even be necessary for you to press the e-court button to see those on your screen as we go through. Your Honours, in 1999 Kosovo was prominent in international headlines with video images of conflict and convoys of thousands and thousands of Kosovar Albanian refugees, women, children, and the elderly, leaving the country on foot or in wagons drawn by tractors. This trial is going to be about the how and the why that human exodus from Kosovo took place and about who was responsible for it. We say that the evidence in this case will show that these six accused, Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, Dragoljub Ojdanic, Nebojsa Pavkovic, Vladimir Lazarevic, and Sreten Lukic, were co-participants with Slobodan Milosevic and other Serbian political, military, and police officials in a joint criminal enterprise, a JCE. And I should tell you here at this point, Your Honours, that I will probably use a number of acronyms during my remarks, and I've got a list here that we'd like to hand around for everybody to use, if we could do that now. I'll have my case manager hand them to the usher. I understand the Defence already have received a copy. The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise, this JCE, was to manipulate or modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to maintain and continue Serbian control over the province of Kosovo. While motive, the why question, is not a necessary element for us to prove in our case, it is a factor that can help you, Your Honours, you Judges, you triers of fact, to understand the evidence. You'll hear evidence about the importance of Kosovo for the Serb leadership, and about the special importance it held for Slobodan Milosevic. In order to best explain what we believe the evidence in this case will show, I'd like to take a journalistic approach to telling you this real-life story, so we'll ask and answer the six basic questions of: What? When? Where? Who? Why? And how? Let me start off with the where question. Well, where is Kosovo. I want to talk for a minute about the geography and the demographics of Kosovo. To begin with it might be helpful to show a couple of maps and talk briefly about the history of this place Kosovo. And during the trial you'll hear it referred to in a variety of ways. Serb witnesses and documents may refer to Kosovo i Metohija or sometimes the acronym KiM. Kosovar Albanians may use the term Kosova, and most internationals and the Prosecution team will use the term Kosovo. Let's have a look at our first map of the area. Do you have that on your screen, Your Honours? Before the wars of the early 1990s, the former Yugoslavia, which was then called the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or the SFRY, looked like this. The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was then made up of six republics and in alphabetical order they were: Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Slovenia. Within Serbian itself, there were two so-called autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo. We'll talk more about autonomous provinces and what the term autonomy meant. Now, as you can see on this map, Kosovo was located in the southern part of the Republic of Serbia, which after the Dayton Peace Agreement of December 1995 was a constituent republic of the federal republic of Yugoslavia. Kosovo is boarded on the north and the north-west by the Republic of Montenegro, on the west and south-west by the Republic of Albania, and to the south by the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Kosovo has been contested territory for much of its history. Kosovo Albanians claim that their ancestors, Illyrians and Dardanians, were the original inhabitants of the area. Serbs, on the other hand, trace the beginnings of their political and religious history to medieval Kosovo. Between 1912 and 1918, and again during World War II, Kosovo was occupied by a number of different forces. At the end of the Second World War, Kosovo was formally annexed to Serb. You will find that Kosovo is a relatively small area geographically. To illustrate this point, I'm going to show you a graphic demonstrating the relative size of Kosovo compared to the Netherlands. Note that Kosovo is barely over 150 kilometres at its widest from one end to the other whichever direction you travel. And next up on the screen for you we've got a map of Kosovo showing the principal towns and cities, including in the right middle the capital city of Pristina. Next up we'll show you another map of Kosovo showing the approximately 30 municipalities into which it was divided. You may note that in our indictment and on some of the maps you'll see during this trial there are alternate spellings listed for the various place names, usually with the Serbian version first, followed by the Albanian. In certain instances the name is the same in both languages, but in others it's quite different. Some witnesses may refer to the Serbian name and some will use the Albanian. We generally, on the Prosecution team, will use the Serbian version so that the accused will be aware of which locations we're talking about. By the end of the trial, I suspect we'll all have a pretty good idea for both the Albanian and Serbian versions of these place names. Speaking now of the towns and the municipalities, who lived in Kosovo? Well, primarily there were two ethnic groups: Albanians and Serbs. Together they made up about 90 per cent of the population. Prior to the conflicts in 1999, the last census with nearly complete participation took place in 1981. At that time, it showed a total population for Kosovo of approximately 1.585.000 citizens, of which 77 per cent were Albanians and 13 per cent were Serbs. The remaining 10 per cent consisted of several different ethnic groups, including Turks, Roma, and a few more, all those lumped together in the category "others." Kosovo Albanians boycotted the census carried out in 1991, but general estimates of the population for Kosovo in 1998 suggest that the total population in Kosovo for that year was in the neighbourhood of 2 to 2.2 million, of which Albanians constituted approximately 85 or 80 to 85 per cent and the Serbs approximately 5 to 10 per cent. These numbers and percentages will be useful for you to remember later on when we talk about the number of Albanians -- Kosovo Albanians forcibly transferred within and deported from Kosovo during 1999. Now, let me move on and talk about the when of this case. I'll give you a brief history and chronology leading up to the 1999 conflict. All the crimes charged in our indictment against these accused, the persecutions, which include rapes, physical assaults, robbery, destruction of property, looting, and destruction of religious and cultural sites, and the murders, the forcible transfers, and the deportations, all these occurred during the first half of 1999. The indictment also alleges that the forces of the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and of Serbia had engaged in similar conduct in 1998. And we'll talk more about that later on. But for a better understanding of that first half of 1999 and the events that occurred then, I need to give you a brief overview of some history of the area. In 1974, a new constitution was passed in the SFRY, which in effect shifted the power from the central federal authority to the six constituent republics we saw on our map earlier, Bosnia, Croatia, Montenegro, Macedonia, Serbia, and Slovenia, and to the two provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo. These powers that were granted under the new constitution included republican, or in case of Vojvodina and Kosovo provincial, control over the judiciary, the police, and the educational system. In addition, Kosovo was given representation in the federal Assembly, the constitutional court, and the Presidency of the SFRY. President Tito of Yugoslavia died in 1980 and political unrest began to stir in Kosovo. In the 1980s, Kosovo Serbs voiced their concerns about discrimination against them by the Albanian majority provincial government. And you will recall the percentages, Albanians in Kosovo were in a big majority. In 1986, the so-called SANA memorandum, S-A-N-A, written by certain Serbia intellectuals from the Serb Academy of Art and Science became public, and that document spoke of a "physical, political, judicial, and cultural genocide of the Serbian population in Kosovo and Metohija." Meanwhile, during this same time period in the 1980s, Kosovo Albanians expressed their concerns about economic underdevelopment in the province. Kosovo Albanians also sought additional political liberalisation and they wanted to have republic status for Kosovo. Beginning in the 1980s and continuing off and on through the 1990s, Kosovo Albanians frequently staged demonstrations which were often forcefully suppressed by military and police forces of Serbia. In 1986 Slobodan Milosevic was on the rise in Yugoslav politics. He was elected chairman of the presidium of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia. In April 1987 he travelled to Kosovo and for him he made what was a seminal speech to local Serbs, which marked his apparent adoption of Serb nationalism. His speech received enormous publicity, and it made him a hero in the eyes of many Serbs. It marked a turning point in his career. We say he rode the rising tide of nationalism in Serbia and came to gain even greater control of the political leadership in the SFRY. In later years, Milosevic came to believe that his political career would come to a sudden end if he gave in to ethnic Albanian demands in Kosovo. As about this same time, the Albanians in Kosovo were continuing to press for greater independence. In October 1988, there were demonstrations against Serb nationalism and over concerns about the continued autonomy of the province. In February 1989, there were massive worker strikes in Kosovo; in particular, by the mine workers. These were against the threats of revocation of Kosovo's autonomy. Slobodan Milosevic and the SFRY Presidency responded strongly to this ongoing unrest in Kosovo. Declaring that the situation had deteriorated to such an extent as to threaten the constitution, the integrity, and the sovereignty of the country, the SFRY Presidency imposed "special measures." These special measures re-assigned police authority and responsibility for public security from the provincial government of Kosovo back to the federal government of the SFRY. On the 23rd of March, 1989, the Kosovo Assembly met and we, the Prosecution, say they met under threat and duress and intimidation, caused, in no small part, by the presence of tanks outside the Assembly building. During that meeting the members voted to give up their control of the police, education, choice of official language, and veto powers over further changes to the Serbian constitution. A few days later the Assembly of Serbia approved those changes to the constitution, and in September 1990 passed this new constitution which revoked the autonomy previously granted to Kosovo in 1974. The courts and the Municipal Councils in Kosovo ceased to function. Not surprisingly, there followed more strikes and demonstrations in Kosovo. These actions were strongly repressed with scores of demonstrators killed and hundreds put on trial. On the 600th anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo, a significant event in the history of Serbs, on the 600th anniversary of that battle, in June 1989, Slobodan Milosevic appeared before a crowd in Gazimestan in Kosovo and made another speech in which he foreshadowed the possibility of armed battles to come. We'd like to play just a short clip from that speech, Your Honours. The audio is in B/C/S and you can hear the speaker and the sounds of the crowd. The English subtitles appear on the screen. So if you want to listen, you'll have to listen over your headphones. If we could play that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the next couple of years following the imposition of these special measures, which discriminated against the Kosovo Albanians and their efforts at greater independence, the political situation in Kosovo grew increasingly tense. Serbia took over complete control of the police, the courts, the educational system, et cetera. Thousands of Kosovo Albanian professionals, doctors, professors, teachers, police, and civil servants, were dismissed from their job. Police violence against Kosovo Albanians was on the rise. In the early 1990s, discriminatory measures were put in place that we say were the early attempts by legislative means to alter the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to maintain Serb control of the province. Just as the Albanian professionals were being removed from their jobs because of their ethnicity, many were replaced by Serbs, whether qualified for the position or not. Indeed, after the outbreak of the wars in Croatia and Bosnia in the early 1990s, a number of Serb refugees from those republics were relocated to Kosovo, and special incentives to lure Serbs to settle in Kosovo were attempted, but this particular effort, this kind of effort to alter the ethnic balance in favour of Serbs in Kosovo, didn't meet with any great success. In July 1990, the Kosovo Assembly passed an unofficial resolution, declaring Kosovo to be an equal and independent entity within the SFRY; that is, equal to the republics of Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia, et cetera. The Assembly of Serbia responded within a matter of days by passing a decision suspending or dissolving the Assembly of Kosovo. Nevertheless, the suspended Kosovo Assembly remained active, and in September 1990 they proclaimed a constitution for their would-be Republic of Kosovo. A year later, in September 1991, the Kosovo Albanians held an unofficial referendum which was overwhelmingly in favour of independence. This action was consistent with what was happening elsewhere within the former Yugoslavia at that time. You will see referendums being held in Bosnia, Croatia. In May 1992, the Kosovo Albanians held unofficial elections for an Assembly and president of their own Republic of Kosovo. Ibrahim Rugova, a founder and member of the Democratic League of Kosovo, Lidhja Demokratike e Kosoves - my Albanian is not very good - called LDK for short in my remarks, Rugova was chosen president and six years later was re-elected to that position. During the early 1990s the LDK led an official coalition government in Kosovo, pursued a policy of non-violent civil resistance and began establishing unofficial parallel institutions in the sectors of education and health care in Kosovo. Meanwhile, what was happening in the rest of Yugoslavia? Well, for one thing, the old League of Communists was losing its strangle-hold as the party of power. And 1990 saw the rise of many new political parties throughout the country, including a number of nationalist parties. Slobodan Milosevic was solidifying his power base. He was chosen as the president of Serbia in December 1990. He also became president of a newly founded Serbian Socialist Party, the SPS. The SPS became the most powerful political party in Serbia and remained so until the year 2000. The power of the party in the former Yugoslavia and in Serbia should not be underestimated. As president of the SPS, Milosevic had enormous de facto power, to hire and fire, to choose who would fill the most important and most powerful positions in the government, in the media, in the banks, in all the important positions in Serbia. Our accused, Milan Milutinovic and Nikola Sainovic, both held prominent positions within the SPS and they owed part of their de facto power to their membership in that party and their personal relationship with Milosevic. Elsewhere, the SFRY was beginning to break up in a succession of wars. First briefly in Slovenia, then in Croatia and Bosnia, where the fighting went on from 1991 and 1992 until the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed in December 1995. It's worth noting that the Dayton Accords made no mention of Kosovo, which was certainly a disappointment for many Kosovo Albanians, who may have held out hope that it might be a time when their quest for independence could be addressed. That disappointment on the part of Kosovo Albanians may help explain subsequent events in Kosovo, in particular, a growing disillusionment on the part of many Kosovo Albanians with Dr. Rugova and the LDK's policy of peaceful, non-violent resistance. Although Rugova managed in 1996 to reach an agreement with Milosevic that would have returned certain educational rights and privileges to the Kosovo Albanians, that agreement was never implemented. At any rate, in the mid-1990s, a faction of Kosovo Albanians organised a group known as Ushtria Clirimtare e Kosoves, or UCK in the Albanian or, as known in English, the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA as we will refer to it, and the KLA, contrary to the position of the LDK, advocated a policy of armed insurgency and violent resistance to the Serb authorities in Kosovo. By mid-1996 the KLA had begun launching armed attacks, primarily against the Serb police forces. The Serb police responded in force with numerous operations against suspected KLA bases and supporters in Kosovo, and the persecution of Kosovo Albanian civilians became more common and widespread. This alternating pattern of aggression by the KLA on the one hand and the forces of the FRY and Serbia on the other continued throughout 1997 and 1998 with an ever-increasing level of violence. You'll note here my use of the term "forces of the FRY and Serbia." As we noted in our indictment and our pre-trial brief, we use that term to include not only units of the Yugoslav army, the VJ, and of the Ministry of Interior, MUP, M-U-P, not just VJ and MUP forces in Kosovo, but also various military territorial units, civil defence units, village defence forces, armed locals, and volunteer units attached to, assigned to, or otherwise incorporated into the VJ and the MUP, and we'll talk more about that when we talk about the who of this case. At the beginning of 1996 and 1997, the KLA was small in numbers, poorly armed, and disorganised. Most of its leadership was abroad. However, due in part to the availability of additional weapons, following a collapse of law and order in neighbouring Albania and an ever-growing number of volunteers, the KLA by 1998 grew to include several thousand members and to become more and more active against the Serb police and also at times against Kosovo Albanians believed to be loyal to the Serb authorities. The conflict intensified, and the Serb response to KLA activities was widely viewed as being disproportionate and amounting to "excessive and indiscriminate force" against Kosovo Albanian civilians. Villages and towns were shelled and residents driven away. Peaceful demonstrations were forcefully subdued -- I'm sorry, peaceful demonstrators were forcefully subdued and arrested. The problem was significant enough to gain the attention of the international community. In March 1998, Serb forces carried out an operation in the Srbica municipality, attacking the village of Donji Prekaz and killing about 50 people, including several women and children of the family of Adem Jashari at their family compound. And when I use the term "compound" here, Your Honours, I'm using it to describe a particular feature of Kosovo Albanian architecture and a fairly common practice of building multi-generational houses surrounded with walls and not to suggest that the Jashari family home was an unusual military fortification of some sort. Also in March 1998 the United Nations Security Council deemed it necessary and appropriate to issue its Resolution 1160, which condemned "the use of excessive force by the Serbian police forces against civilians and peaceful demonstrators in Kosovo." It also condemned activities of violence by the KLA. By May of 1998, as a result of these operations by forces of the FRY and Serbia, approximately 15.000 Kosovo Albanians had fled to Albania and a total of about 28.000 persons had been displaced from their homes. Despite the March 1998 UN resolution condemning these practices, Milosevic and the forces of FRY and Serbia chose not only to continue with their operations against the KLA, including against the civilian population in areas where KLA operated, but to increase the level and the scope of that campaign. In July 1998, the forces of the FRY and Serbia began a large-scale offensive throughout the province of Kosovo. This operation included, among other forces, various brigades of the VJ's Pristina Corps, which was then commanded by our accused General Pavkovic, and special units of the MUP. It's interesting to note here that the month before the launch of this big summer offensive, we see the creation of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, with a mandate to coordinate civil affairs and the activities of the army and the police, the VJ and the MUP. The role and the importance of this Joint Command is reflected in a VJ military order that you'll see during the trial dated the 7th of July, 1998 from the commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade, declaring a ban on operations without the knowledge and approval of the Joint Command. Joint Command meetings occurred on almost a daily basis from July to October 1998 during this big offensive, and three of our accused here, Sainovic, Pavkovic, and Lukic, often attended those meetings. In 1999 we'll see our accused General Lazarevic joining those three in the Joint Command and attending meetings. More about the Joint Command later on when I talk about the who in question. In the face of this continued campaign of disproportionate force against the civilian population in Kosovo, the UN Security Council adopted another resolution on the 23rd of September, 1998. Resolution 1199 called for an immediate cease-fire in Kosovo, an international presence to monitor that cease-fire, and the withdrawal of security forces used for civilian repression. This resolution and the increasing outcry on both the domestic and international fronts forced Milosevic to engage in international negotiations with, among others, US Ambassador Richard Holbrooke and NATO generals Klaus Naumann and Wesley Clark in late 1998. NATO was on the verge of launching air strikes against Serbia if the use of disproportionate and indiscriminate force against the civilian population in Kosovo continued. During the trial you'll hear some detailed evidence about these negotiations which occurred in late October 1998. In addition to Slobodan Milosevic, key participants from the Serb side included MUP General Djordjevic and two of our accused here in court, Milan Milutinovic and Nikola Sainovic. Key provisions insisted on by NATO -- by the NATO team in these negotiations were the secession of disproportionate force against the civilian population and the reduction of VJ and MUP forces in Kosovo. Eventually, after agreeing and signing the document, Milosevic said he would try to find a solution for the Kosovo problem in the spring of 1999 and that a pre-condition for a solution was to achieve balance within or between ethnic groups. There wasn't an explanation of what balance meant in that context. Nikola Sainovic expressed that the problem related to a higher birth-rate among Kosovo Albanians and that they had to find a solution which would not lead to the same problem in a few of years. When Naumann and Clark asked for clarification, Milosevic said they would do the same as they had done in 1945 and 1946 which, as he further explained, was to gather them together and shoot them. Milosevic suggested that the problem would be dealt with in the spring. This 25 October 1998 agreement also called on the creation and deployment of a verification mission from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the OSCE, and it was to be called the Kosovo Verification Mission or KVM, consisting of unarmed observers to deploy in the province, to verify compliance with the terms of that October 25th agreement. You'll hear evidence about the experience of the KVM monitors. A United Nations report noted that by the end of October 1998 approximately 285.000 Kosovo Albanians had been displaced from their homes. You'll remember our numbers about the total population in Kosovo being 2 to 2.2 million with Kosovar Albanians being about 80 to 85 per cent. So do the math and you'll see 285.000 is a significant portion of all Kosovo Albanians living in the province. And these 285.000 had been displaced, either internally within Kosovo, some of them camping out in the mountains and the forests, the fields, or in other villages, and some across the borders of Kosovo to a neighbouring country. 285.000 represents more than 15 per cent of the total population of the province at that time, almost one in every six or seven persons in the country, and this is even before what I would refer to as the main event in 1999. Unfortunately, the October agreements did not achieve the hoped-for results. There were some initial withdrawals of Serb forces in the beginning. However, the KLA quickly moved in to fill the void in those areas and remained active against the forces of FRY and Serbia. By December, the numbers of Serb forces were on the rise again. From their arrival in November 1998 until their departure in March 1999, the KVM observers noted in addition to operations against the KLA, there was ongoing violence by the forces of FRY and Serbia against the civilian population. Another note of interest in the chronology here is that in late 1998, Slobodan Milosevic made certain key personnel changes in the VJ command. In the Prosecution's view, and we believe as will be supported in the anticipated evidence, these changes were in part to replace individuals who had criticised or expressed concern about Milosevic's policy in Kosovo and what they saw as an improper or inappropriate use of the army. The evidence supports the suggestion that the new faces were seen as individuals who were willing to follow the course intended by Milosevic in terms of solving in spring 1999 the Kosovo problem, the Kosovo problem being ethnic imbalance. As a result of these changes, our accused General Ojdanic became chief of the General Staff of the VJ. General Pavkovic was elevated from commander of the Pristina Corps to command the 3rd Army, and Vladimir Lazarevic moved up from his position of Chief of Staff to become the commander of the 3rd Army subordinate unit in Kosovo, the Pristina Corps. Additional changes were made in regard to senior officers in 1999 for similar reasons. We say these moves were not limited to the VJ but also took place in the MUP, in the police, where Radomir Markovic was named to replace Jovica Stanisic as head of the State Security Service, RDB being the acronym for that. And more about the MUP and the RDB when we discuss the who question later on. An operation by the forces of the FRY and Serbia in mid-January 1999 led over 40 Kosovar Albanians dead in Racak and gained international attention when the head of the Kosovo Verification Mission visited the site and made public statements about it. This event helped spur ongoing efforts to stop the violence in Kosovo. Further international efforts to resolve the crisis resulted in an international peace conference in Rambouillet and Paris, France, in February 1999. Representatives for the Serb side included Nikola Sainovic and Milan Milutinovic. The Albanians were represented by their non-officially elected representatives, Ibrahim Rugova, for one. There was also a delegation of the KLA involved in the talks. During these negotiations the fighting in Kosovo continued, and Serb forces began to mass on the borders of Kosovo. The would-be peace talks eventually collapsed in mid-March 1999. With the failure of these negotiations, the KVM verifiers withdrew from Kosovo. On 23 March 1999, a declaration of an imminent threat of war was proclaimed in the FRY. The very next day, 24 March 1999, a "state of war" was declared and the NATO bombs began to fall in Kosovo and elsewhere in Serbia. Members of the joint criminal enterprise had already recognised as early as February 1999 that there would be a window of opportunity when NATO attacked, a window of opportunity for them to achieve their aim of modifying the ethnic balance under the guise of crushing the KLA. When that window did open, they acted swiftly by launching large joint operations using the forces of the FRY and Serbia, the VJ and the MUP. The JCE's objective of modifying the ethnic balance to maintain Serb control in the province, that is by depopulating Kosovo of as many Kosovo Albanians as possible in the course of the conflict with NATO, was largely achieved by early April, although some more isolated operations continued to occur after this. And we'll talk in some more detail about the deportations and killings alleged in the indictment when I talk about the what question, but first I think now would be a good time to move to the who question. Who? Who were the major players in this story? Now, let's talk about what we expect the evidence to show regarding the most important individuals and organisations involved in bringing about the events underlying the crimes charged in our indictment. First of all, Slobodan Milosevic. No account of the conflict in Kosovo in 1999 could be told without mentioning him. He was the president of the FRY. He was the undisputed political leader and, without question, the most powerful individual in the country. At the time these crimes were alleged in our indictment, his role in the joint criminal enterprise was the boss-man, the one who gave orders, the primary planner and instigator. Milosevic surrounded himself with loyal followers who shared his views about the importance of Kosovo to Serbia and who could be counted on to take the necessary actions to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to maintain Serbian control of the province. As president of the FRY and president of the leading party, the SPS, he had significant de jure and de facto ability to affect and control hirings, firings, and promotions within the various organs of the government, the military, and the police, and he used that ability to assure that he had like-minded people in positions of power. We spoke earlier about the importance that Kosovo held for Milosevic. It was the place where his rise to power began. He also believed that his ability to stay in power during and after the wars in Croatia and Bosnia depended in part on maintaining control in and over Kosovo. During various negotiations with internationals, Milosevic told them that Kosovo was more important than his own head. Milan Milutinovic. Milan Milutinovic was a high-ranking member of the SPS and a close associate of Slobodan Milosevic. He was the president of Serbia from December 1997 until December 2002. As the president of Serbia, he was one of only three voting members on the Supreme Defence Council, the SDC, and we'll talk more about the SDC this a bit. During a declared state of war, which we know came into existence in the FRY on 24 March 1999, the highest leadership body became the "Supreme Command" which we will also speak about a little bit later. President Milutinovic was also a member of the Supreme Command. Milutinovic's prominent position as president of Serbia, as a member of the Supreme Defence Council and the Supreme Command, together with his close relationship with Milosevic and his high status in the SPS, the party in power, all combined to give him substantial de jure and de facto influence and control over the army and the other organs and individuals engaged in implementing the objectives of this joint criminal enterprise. He exercised his authority to assist Milosevic in appointing and promoting other members of the JCE to positions of high authority within the VJ. His contributions to the joint criminal enterprise included being Milosevic's front man, his public face to act as an intermediary with various internationals and diplomats. One example of this is his role in the 1999 February negotiations in Rambouillet. He also made a key contribution to the objective of the JCE by issuing on 31 March 1999, one week of the bombing, started by issuing "decree on identification cards in time of war." You'll hear more details about that when we talk about the deportation crimes. But next I want to talk about another important individual, Nikola Sainovic. By many accounts, Nikola Sainovic was an even closer associate of Slobodan Milosevic. He was considered part of the inner circle. He was also a high-ranking member of the SPS. From 1994 to 2000, he held the post of Deputy Prime Minister of the FRY. In 1998 and 1999, Sainovic was Milosevic's personal choice, delegated with primary responsibility for Kosovo matters. International diplomats wishing to speak with FRY authorities regarding Kosovo were referred to Sainovic. He acted as head of the Joint Command for Kosovo i Metohija in 1999. Sainovic was also a frequent participant at high-level negotiations with international diplomats and others on Kosovo matters. He acted as chair of the FRY Commission for Cooperation with the Kosovo Verification Mission, and he was an active participant in the October 1998 negotiations with NATO and the February 1999 talks in Rambouillet. We say that as Deputy Prime Minister of the FRY and Slobodan Milosevic's designated representative for Kosovo matters, as head of the Joint Command, Nikola Sainovic exercised authority and effective control over the forces of FRY and Serbia which were operating on the ground in Kosovo during 1999. Next we'll talk about Dragoljub Ojdanic. From June 1996 to November 1998, General Ojdanic held the position of Deputy Chief of Staff of the VJ. On 24 November 1998, he was appointed by Slobodan Milosevic to replace General Perisic as Chief of the General Staff. As Chief of the VJ's General Staff, he was the highest ranking, most authoritative uniformed officer in the VJ. From the VJ's 1997 Manual of Command and Control it states that "the commandants of the armies, the air force, and the anti-aircraft defence and the navy are responsible to the chief of the General Staff of the army, as are the commandants of units and temporary compositions immediately subordinate to him." He also acted as chair of the VJ collegium. General Ojdanic, as chief of VJ's Main Staff, was also a member of the SDC, the Supreme Defence Council, and after the state of war was declared on 24 March 1999 he was a member of the Supreme Command and he headed up the Supreme Command Staff. As chief of the General Staff of the VJ and as a member during wartime of the Supreme Command and the Supreme Command Staff, General Ojdanic exercised command authority and effective control over the VJ and units subordinated to it. In particular, he had command and control over the VJ's army, commanded by General Pavkovic, and the Pristina Corps, units operating in Kosovo during 1999, the Pristina Corps commanded by General Lazarevic. In addition, after 23 March 1999, during a state of war, under the FRY Law on Defence, Ojdanic as Chief of the Supreme Command Staff exercised control over MUP units engaged in combat operations as well as other organs subordinated to or acting in concert with the VJ. Next, General Pavkovic, Nebojsa Pavkovic. From January 1998 through 25 December 1998, General Pavkovic was commander of the Pristina Corps of the VJ's 3rd Army. On 25 December 1998 he was appointed by Presidential Decree as commander of the 3rd Army. He took up those duties on 13th of January, 1999, and he remained in that post throughout 1999. Pavkovic was also a member and participant in the Joint Command in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999. Pavkovic had close personal ties with Slobodan Milosevic. He also shared Milosevic's attitude about the importance of Kosovo for Serbia. He publicly stated that "Serbian roots are in Kosovo and everything that is connected to the Serbs throughout the past centuries is there." Pavkovic's attitude toward the Kosovo crisis was set out in a July 1998 letter to his superiors, in which he bemoans the failure to engage the VJ in a more vigorous role in Kosovo, and he speaks of the "loss of Kosovo and the genocide of the Serbs." As commander of the VJ's 3rd Army, General Pavkovic exercised command authority and effective control over the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, and other armed units in Kosovo subordinated to the VJ during 1999. And according to the FRY Law on Defence, after the declaration of a state of war on 24 March 1999, he also had de jure control over MUP units engaged in combat operations in Kosovo. Next on your screen you'll see General Lazarevic. During 1998, Vladimir Lazarevic was Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps in Kosovo. On 25 December 1998, when his immediate superior, General Pavkovic, was elevated to command the 3rd Army, Lazarevic was appointed by Presidential Decree to become commander of the Pristina Corps. He was an active member and participant in the Joint Command in Kosovo. As the commander of the Pristina Corps, Vladimir Lazarevic exercised command authority and effective control over the VJ's Pristina Corps and other units subordinated to it in Kosovo during the time period of the indictment. And next on your screen Sreten Lukic. From May 1998 throughout 1999, Sreten Lukic was head of the MUP staff for Kosovo. As such, he was the ranking MUP official on the ground in Kosovo. He commanded MUP operations in Kosovo and was also a member/participant in the Joint Command. As head of the MUP staff for Kosovo, Sreten Lukic exercised command authority and effective control over MUP units deployed in Kosovo and those units subordinated to the MUP in connection with operations in Kosovo. Now, I've talked about all our accused present here in the courtroom, but I need to talk some more about a few individuals named as being participants in the joint criminal enterprise. First of all, Vlastimir Djordjevic. Djordjevic was a part of this original indictment, as you know. Unfortunately, Mr. Djordjevic apparently will not be with us during this trial. Although he's been indicted, he remains a fugitive and we haven't been able to yet obtain his presence. Vlastimir Djordjevic was assistant minister of internal affairs of the Republic of Serbia. He was the chief of the Public Security Sector, the RJB, another acronym I hope we'll all become familiar with, and that's the uniformed side of the police. We'll talk more about the RJB and some of its special units when we discuss the MUP in a few minutes. Djordjevic reported directly to the minister of the interior, and he was the accused Sreten Lukic's direct superior. Here you see all these folks on an organisational chart showing the Supreme Command. We'll put that up again in a minute, but I want to finish with a couple of key players and we'll come back to this. Vlajko Stojiljkovic was the minister of internal affairs of Serbia from March 1998 until October 2000. He is since deceased, but we allege that he was a member of the JCE and he will be mentioned often during the trial. As the minister of internal affairs, he was the boss of the MUP. He directed the work of the MUP and its personnel during the time-frame of this indictment. Next, Obrad Stevanovic. Obrad Stevanovic was also a member of the Ministry of the Interior. He was on the public security side of the house, the RJB. He headed up a subunit of the RJB called the police administration, and you'll hear him mentioned often in this trial in connection with the uniformed special units operating in Kosovo. And one more, Radomir Markovic. He was also an assistant minister of the MUP on the same level as Djordjevic. He was the chief of the State Security Division, the RDB, as opposed to the public security, RJB. These were mostly the plain-clothes police operatives, the secret police, if you will, primarily involved in the collection of information and intelligence related to state security of the Republic of Serbia, but you'll hear later that they did have a uniformed unit that participated. Now, let me talk about some of the organisations or units, groups, involved in the events in 1999. The Yugoslav Army, the VJ. On your screen now you should have an organisational chart showing the command structure of the army. At the top you'll see General Ojdanic as Chief of the General Staff during peacetime and Chief of the Supreme Command Staff after declaration of a state of war on 24 March 1999. He was, if you will, the top dog in the uniformed military chain of command. One of his direct subordinates, and you'll see on this chart immediately below him, was General Pavkovic, commander of the 3rd Army. One level further down on the chain and on the right-hand side of the chart, you'll see another of our accused, General Lazarevic, then the commander of the Pristina Corps which had primary responsibility for the area of Kosovo. Beneath him you'll see some 20 different brigades, battalions, et cetera, of infantry, armour, and special forces. The Yugoslav Army, the VJ, its overall controlling body was the General Staff, which, as I said, during a state of war became the Supreme Command or the Supreme Command Staff. The following strategic groups were subordinate to the General Staff of the army: The 1st Army, the 2nd Army, the 3rd Army, the air and air defence forces, and the navy. In Kosovo, it was units of General Pavkovic's 3rd Army that were active during the time-frame of this indictment. In particular, Kosovo was the primary area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps under General Lazarevic. If I occasionally use the generic term "the army" or "soldiers" I'm referring to elements or personnel of the VJ. The VJ was a modern, professional army. The right of command in the VJ belonged to the FRY president, Milosevic, and to designated officers, including the Chief of the General Staff, Ojdanic, and commanding officers of the units, Pavkovic for the 3rd Army, Lazarevic for the Pristina Corps, et cetera. Command in the VJ was based on the principles of unity of command, singleness of command, and the obligations to carry out lawful orders of a superior. The exercise of command in the VJ included the development of plans and the production of orders by the General Staff. Direction, including orders, was issued by the General Staff on the authority of Ojdanic as its chief, they went to the 3rd Army, Pavkovic. The 3rd Army continued the same process and passed direction and orders down to the Pristina Corps and General Lazarevic, which in turn issued orders to its subordinate brigades and battalions. This is a standard core process in a professional army in which a superior headquarters develops plans and provides direction and orders to suborder units which were carried out at each level in the VJ hierarchy and is common, as I said, to any professional army. So we have direction and orders from the highest level of command being transformed ultimately into combat and other operations on the ground in Kosovo. Many of the VJ's operations were conducted with the MUP and/or with military-territorial units and coordinated through the Joint Command. The VJ also had a system of military discipline and justice, and we'll talk more about that in a later discussion about criminal liable under Article 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal for failure to prevent or punish crimes by subordinates. Next we'll talk about the MUP, the Ministry of Interior, or the police. On your screen you have an organisational chart. The Ministry of Interior was mandated by Serbian law to protect human lives and the safety of persons and their possessions and to maintain law and order. I may occasionally use the generic term "police" by which I mean units and/or personnel of the MUP. You'll see the minister at the top. You'll see that the MUP had two main branches: The Public Security Division, that is the uniformed division, the RJB, headed by the fugitive, Vlastimir Djordjevic, and the State Security Division, the RDB, the secret police, headed by Radomir Markovic. In addition to the regular uniform police which did the regular day-to-day police work we all know about, crime prevention and investigation, enforcement of traffic laws, et cetera, the RJB side of the MUP also had a number of special units which were heavily armed and specially trained and equipped to conduct operations, including combat, and which kinds of things could not be done by the regular police force. In Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, the following specials were actively engaged. And on the RJB side of the house under MUP staff you'll see three blocks. The Special Police Units, or the PJP; the Operational Sweep Groups, the OPG; and the special anti-terrorist unit, the SAJ. Over on the other side of the house in the Ministry of Interior, the state security side under Rade Markovic in the RDB, even though it was primarily an intelligence and information gathering body, it also had its own special unit which wore uniforms and engaged in combat operations in Kosovo. This RDB special unit was called the Special Operations Unit with the acronym JSO. On the chart, as I said, you'll see all four of these falling under the MUP staff, recall that Sreten Lukic was the head of the MUP staff in Kosovo at this time. In addition to all this, the MUP had reservists to supplement its regular contingent. MUP reservists of Serb ethnicity formed the core of local defence units established in many parts of Kosovo. As I said, within Kosovo province, the standard work of the MUP was divided on a geographical basis. There were seven separate regional headquarters called Secretariats of the Interiors, or SUPs, I hate to give you another acronym, but S-U-P. The SUPs, for short, were responsible for the public security task in the municipalities making up the Kosovo province. On your screen you should see the regional SUPs. And now we'll put up another one to show you the municipalities that were covered by each of these seven regional SUPs. Next I want to talk about the Supreme Defence Council. The 1992 FRY constitution places primary responsibility for the defence of the country with the SDC, the president of the FRY and the VJ. In 1999 the SDC was composed of the president of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic; the president of Montenegro, Milos Djukanovic; and the FRY president, Slobodan Milosevic. Those were the only three voting members of the SDC. General Ojdanic, as Chief of the General Staff of the army, was one of the non-voting members of the SDC. The SDC was the highest authority responsible for strategic matters relating to the defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Its mandate under the FRY constitution was to decide upon matters of national defence, including the national defence plan, and the careers of general officers of the VJ. Now if we can go back to the diagram we had before, we'll talk about the Supreme Command. During a state of war, as we said beginning 24 March 1999, the Supreme Command became the highest military-civilian leadership body in the FRY. In effect, it takes the place of the SDC. It was headed by Slobodan Milosevic as Supreme Commander. It formulated strategy and issued directions and commanded operations by the forces of the FRY and Serbia during the declared state of war. Other members of the Supreme Command included Milutinovic, Ojdanic, and the FRY minister of defence. During the state of war, the VJ General Staff became the Supreme Command Staff, again with General Ojdanic as its chief. The direction provided by the Supreme Commander, Milosevic, determined the activities of both the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff, General Ojdanic, and the head of the Joint Command, Nikola Sainovic, and all units under their command, control, and direction. Let me speak for a moment about the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. The Joint Command were Kosovo and Metohija was set up in June 1998. This is about the time of the big summer operation I spoke of earlier, and it continued to function during the first half of 1999. It got its direction from President Milosevic. Its role was to coordinate civil affairs and the activities of the VJ, the MUP, and other armed organisations and groups in Kosovo. In the beginning, it was headed by Milomir Minic, a high-ranking member of the SPS and of Milosevic's inner circle, but then Nikola Sainovic became the de facto head of the Joint Command. Other members or participants included Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Sreten Lukic, as well as the head of the local Temporary Executive Committee, a man named Zoran Andjelkovic. Now, the Joint Command was not a body provided for in the FRY constitution or in the statutory scheme of the FRY or of Serbia. It had the endorsement, however, of Slobodan Milosevic and it was accepted by the other members of the joint criminal enterprise. The Joint Command was responsible for ensuring that the forces of the FRY and Serbia in Kosovo carried out operations in a coordinated manner and in accordance with the political objectives of the leadership, that is of Milosevic and his fellow members of the JCE --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise interfering and bothering you. It means that this Joint Command was not in the text of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. The Joint Command was closely involved in the planning, execution, and monitoring of the various combat operations in Kosovo during the first half of 1999. In effect, the Joint Command brought together the two separate chains of command of the VJ and the MUP that you see on the screen. Now, let's have a look at one of our accused had to say about the Joint Command. In June 2001 in the context of a public debate between our accused General Pavkovic and General Sreten Lukic, General Pavkovic had the following to say about the Joint Command and its role in connection with the VJ and the MUP. "The police had their own headquarters, headed by their own officers, and the cooperation with the army was coordinated through political actors in Joint Command formed for the purpose. Therefore, the information to what the police force units were doing can best be provided by the police commanders and the members of the Joint Command in charge of them." At this point I should alert Your Honours to the existence of another body in Serbia that was sometimes referred to as Joint Command. During 1998 and 1999 in Belgrade in Serbia there was another ad hoc body composed of high-ranking political, military, and police officials which met and discussed matters relating to the events and actions in Kosovo. The participants in this body included Milosevic, Sainovic, Ojdanic, and Pavkovic, among others. Now, this body had no apparent basis in law nor an official title. In addition to being referred to as "Joint Command," it was sometimes also referred to as the "State Commission" or the "Inter-Departmental Staff for the Suppression of Terrorism." This group met in Belgrade and is to be distinguished from the Joint Command in Kosovo that met in Pristina in Kosovo during 1998 and 1999. When we, the Prosecution team, use the term "Joint Command," we'll be talking about the body that met in Kosovo, even though many of the same people were on both -- both groups. We refer to "Joint Command" to mean the body that met in Kosovo. References to the Belgrade group will be specifically identified in another fashion if we talk about that. The MUP staff in Kosovo was located in Pristina and from June 1998 until June 1999 was headed by Sreten Lukic. Its purpose was to manage the work of MUP on the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and to organise and direct the work of MUP units when performing more complex security tasks in the province. Other members of the MUP staff in Kosovo included RDB, state security, secret police department heads in Kosovo, as well as the chiefs of the seven regional MUPs in Kosovo. As head of staff of the MUP in Kosovo, Sreten Lukic was required to report to the minister of internal affairs. Daily situation reports went to, among others, the minister, the assistant ministers heading the RJB and the RDB, that is Vlastimir Djordjevic, the uniformed side of the house, and Rade Markovic, the secret police side of the house. In addition to those regular daily reports, the seven regional SUP chiefs were required to report significant events, not only to the MUP staff in Pristina and General Lukic, but also directly to MUP headquarters in Belgrade. This reporting regime was supplemented by the fact that MUP higher-ups, such as the minister himself, the RJB public security head, Djordjevic; and the head of police administration, that is Obrad Stevanovic; and Nikola Sainovic often attended regular meetings with the MUP staff for Kosovo. At these meetings, Sainovic not only passed on direction from above but was also able to gain information about the situation on the ground and pass it up to Milosevic. I have one more, Your Honour, before the break if that's convenient. I want to briefly mention the TEC, or the Temporary Executive Council, which you will hear mention of. The TEC was created by the Serbian National Assembly in 1998 with the proclaimed purpose of strengthening the work of the civilian structures in Kosovo. It had significant powers over provincial administration authorities. Zoran Andjelkovic, the Serbian minister for youth and sports and also a high-ranking member of the SPS, was named the president of the Temporary Executive Council. He also attended meetings of the Joint Command in Pristina. The evidence will show that our accused were members of one or more of these various organs described in my foregoing remarks and, as such, they made various contributions to the joint criminal enterprise with the intention that the objective of modifying the ethnic balance in a way to ensure Serbian control over Kosovo would be achieved. Detailed descriptions of the various contributions to the JCE by each of the individual accused are set forth in our pre-trial brief and you'll hear more about them during the trial. But for now, I think that's enough to answer the who question before I move on to the what. And, Your Honours, if it's convenient, this would be a good moment to take a break, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is convenient, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll adjourn now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. When we broke, Your Honours, I just finished speaking about the who, and we've already talked about the where and the when. Now I want to talk about the what and how regarding the charged crimes. These accused are charged with persecutions, forced transfers, deportations, and murders committed in the first half of 1999 in Kosovo. The evidence will show that during the time period of our indictment there was an ongoing armed conflict in Kosovo, at first between the forces of the FRY and Serbia on one hand and the KLA on the other; later, between the forces of the FRY and Serbia on the one hand and NATO and the KLA on the other. During this conflict, thousands of Kosovo Albanian civilians and non-combatants were killed by forces of the FRY and Serbia. As many as 800.000 were forcibly transferred and/or deported from Kosovo, and 800.000, that's more than one in three of the total population of Kosovo Albanians estimated to be living in Kosovo at the time -- actually, it's one in three of the total population, rechecking my math, and one in two of the Kosovo Albanian population. Although our indictment begins with 1 January 1999, you will know from the indictment and the pre-trial brief and my earlier comments on the chronology leading up to 1999, that the crimes in 1999 are just the final chapter in a campaign of persecutions that -- and escalating violence that -- engaged in by the forces of Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia and their leaders to try and maintain physical and political control of the province of Kosovo in the face of ever-growing demands by Kosovo Albanians for increased autonomy or independence. With the onset of the NATO bombing, the forces of FRY and Serbia stepped up their programme to remove the Kosovo Albanians. In only one week, the very first week of the war, between 24 and 30 March 1999, the United Nations data reflects that some 94.000 Kosovars fled Kosovo. Many reported that they didn't know where their men were, as they had been separated from them at the time they were expelled. Many reported that they had been deliberately expelled and explicitly told to leave and they also reported their homes had been destroyed by the Serb forces. Many reported that they had to leave on little or no notice at all, forced to flee at night, on foot, in freezing temperatures, often with nothing more than the clothes on their backs and whatever few things they could carry in their hands as they rushed out the door. Many reported having been rounded up by the Serb forces and put on trains or buses to be taken to the border for expulsion to Albania or to Macedonia. Some of the very young and the very old died during this mass exodus. Your Honours, at this juncture we'd like to show you a brief video depicting some scenes of the Kosovo Albanians leaving Kosovo. I think the total time is less than two minutes, and we'll play it now without any audio. And these segments are all from video excerpts we intend to introduce at the trial later on. So if we could play that video. The first is a refugee convoy at the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see them in the convoys and the tractors pulling wagons full of people. Next we have some of the refugees walking along the railway line from Kosovo into Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next segment shows them on -- getting on the train to go to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also walking on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next one shows them in arriving in -- gathering in a field once they've left Kosovo. And the last one is a scene of one of the camps on the Kosovo-Macedonia border, showing the thousands of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, it's quite possible that there will be a suggestion that these people left because of the NATO bombing rather than because of attacks by the forces of the FRY and Serbia. We submit that the evidence will show that the vast majority of these refugees fled because of the VJ, the actions of the army and the police and the other forces of the FRY and Serbia, not because of the NATO bombs. Many of the Kosovo Albanian witnesses will tell you they welcomed the NATO bombing. Of particular assistance to the Chamber in this regard in dealing with this issue will be the evidence of an expert witness, Dr. Patrick Ball, who testified in the Milosevic case. In his expert report, he specifically addresses this question of whether the refugee flows were the result of the actions of the forces of the FRY and Serbia, the NATO bombing, or the KLA activity. His conclusion corroborates the evidence of the crime base witnesses whom we intend to present, which is that they left as a direct consequence of the acts of the forces of the FRY and Serbia, not because of the NATO bombing, not because of the KLA activity. At this point in time, 24th of March, 1999, immediately following the evacuation of the KVM monitors and with the beginning of the NATO bombing, the forces of the FRY and Serbia had a perfect opportunity to step up their campaign of ethnic removal and at the same time to be able to claim that others were to blame for the departure of the Kosovo Albanians. We contend that the evidence and the witnesses will show that this is exactly what they did do. All across Kosovo in a concerted and coordinated manner, the forces of the FRY and Serbia began their widespread and systematic attack on the Kosovo Albanian civilian population, going from one tiny village to the next and from one town to another, murdering, beating, robbing, looting, destroying businesses and mosques, and forcing out the Kosovar Albanians in front of them. They burned and destroyed villages or towns as they went in order to leave nothing behind for those expelled to return to. The evidence will show a typical pattern occurred in which the Serb forces would nearly encircle a town or village, leaving one avenue of escape. The VJ would commence shelling with artillery and heavy weapons. Then the MUP units, including special units and volunteers, incorporated or otherwise attached to the MUP or VJ, would enter the town, force the people out, sometimes killing or raping as they did so, and often looting and then burning the abandoned houses. This kind of activity understandably created an atmosphere of terror, and the inhabitants of neighbouring villages seeing this happen and hearing the stories of the primary victims would join in fleeing to avoid a similar fate as that suffered by their neighbours. And so the massive convoys seen in the international media quickly came into existence from the end of March 1999 as thousands and thousands of Kosovo Albanians literally fled for their very lives. In this regard, you may also hear a suggestion that the forces of FRY and Serbia were not forcing civilians out but instead were merely escorting them to safety to the borders, where they were voluntarily seeking to go to avoid the NATO bombing. The evidence will refute that suggestion. Of particular note on this point is the evidence of many witnesses about how en route out of the country and at the borders, forces of the FRY and Serbia regularly forced the refugees to hand over their identity documents, and they took the vehicle licence plates off their tractors and their cars and the wagons before they'd left Kosovo and went into Albania or Macedonia. To what purpose would that be if they indeed were only be escorted to temporary safety? Why would they or should they surrender their identity documents upon leaving the province? We suggest it's a clear manifestation of the joint criminal enterprise's objective to modify the ethnic balance of Kosovo in order to maintain Serb control. Once outside the country and with no official identity documents, how were those refugees going to be able to return to Kosovo under Serb authorities who could simply say: Sorry, it looks like you're simply an illegal immigrant from Albania. You can't come in now. You'll remember earlier when I was discussing President Milutinovic and his contribution to the joint criminal enterprise, we mentioned the decree on identification cards in time of war. I'd like to put that up on your screen now and have a quick look at that. You'll see it provided that any persons who "lose their identity cards or are otherwise left without them" are obliged to report this within 24 hours to the organisational unit of the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP, which has jurisdiction in the place where the identity card was lost. It goes on to say those persons then are obliged to request a new card in their place of residence within eight days. Now, think about that as a practical matter. How would this work in real life for the tens of thousands of Kosovo Albanians being forced from their homes in the spring of 1999? What sense in reporting the loss of your identity card to the local MUP when your card is being taken by you by a local policeman? And who would dare turn around and travel back to their home village, in the light of what they had just witnessed, to apply for a new card? To even do so under the circumstances would have been sheer folly and maybe even downright suicidal. The logical inference from all of this conduct and the timing of this decree is that there was an intention that those Kosovar Albanians, once removed, would not be allowed to return, thus effecting the desired modification of the ethnic balance necessary to solve the Kosovo problem. The indictment reflects the widespread nature of this campaign. Our indictment includes 12 killing sites, which now we'll be leading the evidence of nine on, and 13 deportation sites. This is not a complete list of all crimes that allegedly happened in Kosovo or were reported to investigators, rather these were selected as a representative sample sufficient to show the existence of a pattern and to reflect the scope and nature of the campaign throughout the province of Kosovo. First I'd like to talk about what we refer to as the killing sites. Now on your screen we'd like to show you a map with red circles for the locations of the killing sites listed in the indictment. I'm not going to talk about each and every one, but I do want to talk about some of them. First of all, I want to talk about Bela Crkva. Bela Crkva was in Orahovac municipality, and the alleged crimes occurred there on the 25th of March, the day after the beginning of the NATO bombing. Forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the village of Bela Crkva in Orahovac. Many of the villagers fled along a small river and hid under a railroad bridge. Serbian police opened fire on one group of villagers hiding under the bridge, killing 12 people, ten of them women and children. The remaining villagers were ordered out of the streambed and out from under the bridge. The men and the older boys were separated, ordered to strip, and then they were robbed of their valuables and their identity documents. The women were then ordered to leave, to go to another nearby village. The village doctor tried to intercede with the police commander, but he and his nephew were shot and killed on the spot. The remaining boys and men then were ordered back into the streambed. The Serb forces opened fire, killing most of them. A few survivors lived to tell the tale. The village was destroyed. Later exhumations confirmed the deaths of over 50 villagers from Bela Crkva. And I'd like to put up on the screen for you an aerial photo of Bela Crkva. On the left you see a photo of the village on the 11th of March, 1999, two weeks before the attack; and on the right is the 2nd of April, a week after. You'll see the damage to the buildings. You'll see the note at the bottom of the image indicated that the image on the right is rotated 180 degrees, and I'm sorry we weren't able to fix that before we started. But you can see the river on the right-hand side of the right image; you'll see on the left-hand side that the river is on the left. So if in your minds you can flip the right half of the image upside down, you'll see that the features match up the river, the big white building in the middle, et cetera. Now, let's go to Mala Krusa. Mala Krusa is also located in the municipality of Orahovac. Also on the day after the NATO bombing began, just a few kilometres down the road from Bela Crkva, the forces of the FRY and Serbia were attacking the villages of Mala Krusa and Velika Krusa. The villagers fled into the nearby forest, and they could see the attackers looting and burning their homes. The next morning, the 26th of March, the Serb forces located many of the villagers on the outskirts of town. They ordered the women and children to leave and to go to Albania. The men and older boys were detained, searched, and robbed of their valuables and their identity documents. The forces of FRY and Serbia then forced the men and older boys into a nearby house and began shooting at them with machine-guns. They then set fire to the house. Approximately 100 were killed in this massacre. Next I want to talk about Suva Reka. Suva Reka on the 26th of March, the same day as the attack in Mala Krusa, forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded the Berisha family compound in the Suva Reka town, and they ordered the occupants to come out. At that time six of the men were killed on the spot. The remaining family members were forced down the street into a coffee shop. Once inside, they were fired upon by the Serb forces. Several women and children. Explosives were then thrown into the shop where the victims were, and we have just a short video showing you the shop where this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the coffee shop where the Berisha family members were taken to and shot, and all -- at least 44 persons were killed, including 15 women and 15 children. Bodies of the victims were then thrown into the rear of a truck, which drove off toward Prizren. Amazingly, three survivors of this horrific attack, two women and an 8-year-old boy, pretending to be dead and having been thrown into the truck with the others, managed to crawl out and escape from among that truckload of the dead. And you'll hear testimony from one of those women. You will also hear about where some of those dead victims ended up. Remains of the Berisha family members killed on that day were found in two different locations: Some at a firing range in Prizren municipality, and others in clandestine mass grave site by the training centre for the SAJ, the elite anti-terrorist unit of the Serbian MUP, one of the special units we told you about before; at Batajnica, near Belgrade in Serbia. And here I want to pause for a moment and show you a graphic to emphasise an important point that we believe the evidence will show. You'll see the distance from Suva Reka to Batajnica is approximately equal to the difference from The Hague to a point in Luxembourg, approximately 285 kilometres. How did those bodies get from Suva Reka to that hole in the ground near Belgrade, some 285 kilometres away? And not just any old piece of ground, but police property, an area with limited, restricted access, the training centre for the special unit, the anti-terrorist SAJ. And why? Why would dead Albanian civilians, women and children, be taken away and hidden away like that? Who could have done that? Who had the means and opportunity to do that? And what motive to go to such logistical lengths during a state of war, the time when resources like men and trucks and fuel must have been precious, given the ongoing NATO bombing and combat with KLA. We suggest that this evidence shows the intent of the accused that forces under their control should implement the solution for the Kosovo problem along the lines suggested by Milosevic in his remarks to Clark and Naumann in October 1998 during the negotiations. We say it also reflects guilty knowledge on their part that these killings were not part of a legitimate anti-terrorist campaign, but rather a criminal enterprise to modify the ethnic balance in order to maintain Serb control of Kosovo. Next up I want to show you Izbica in Srbica municipality. On the 28th of March, a couple of days later, in Srbica municipality, forces of the FRY and Serbia had begun firing heavy weapons on several villages in the area near the village of Izbica. As many as 4500 people fleeing from these attacks had gathered in a field near Izbica. On the 28th of March, forces of the FRY and Serbia had surrounded these displaced Kosovo Albanian civilians. They approached and demanded money. The women and children were ordered to leave and go to Albania. Two disabled elderly women seated in a trailer who were unable to walk, Serb forces set fire to the trailer and burned those women alive. The men were separated from the women and children and then the men were divided into two groups. One group was taken towards the woods and a stream, where they were then told to kneel down. And then the Serb forces began shooting them. The second group was marched off in another direction, made to line up, before they, too, were shot. Miraculously there were survivors from both these mass shootings, and you will hear live from at least one of them with evidence from others proposed to be submitted in written form or otherwise they'll attend here for cross-examination at least. Over 100 men were killed on that day in Izbica, and you will hear live, as I said, from one of the survivors of the massacre. Local villagers then gathered up the dead and buried them. A local doctor named Liri Loshi filmed the bodies for identification, and you'll see that in full later in the evidence, and you'll hear from Liri Loshi. As I said, the victims were then buried in Izbica by the villagers, but they didn't stay buried for long. At any rate, by sometime between mid-May and the 3rd of June, 1999, the Izbica killing victims were dug up out of what had presumably been thought to be their final resting place. And we'd like to show you some aerial photos now to explain this. Two images on your screen. On the left half is Izbica, Kosovo, on the 9th of March, 1999. In the upper right centre, you'll see an area marked as "no graves." And in the right middle something marked as "no vehicles and debris." On the right half of your screen is an image showing the same area on the 15th of April, and in that area there are now graves. And in the lower right you'll see vehicles and debris being described as appearing in that image. From the testimony of the witnesses you will understand where the vehicles and the debris are mentioned is where the 4500 who had previously fled from surrounding villages were camping and staying when this happened. If we could go to the next image. This is from the 3rd of June, 1999, from the same area. On the insert you'll see something says "see following graphic." This is area where the graves were on the previous image. We'll go to a close-up. On the left half of this image is the area where the graves were on the 15th of May, 1999; and on the right, that same area on the 3rd of June. With a big dark area indicating disturbed earth. No neat rows of individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a little question for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.text: Sorry for interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Please, you said the graves were later dug out. Is it only what you want to say or the bodies were --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have some more to say on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Not now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Because it leaves a bit of a vacuum. After the two words --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hope I can clear it up in just a moment.

utterances.text: That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see now on June 3rd it appears that the earth has been disturbed. On the 27th of June, 1999, a French forensic team went to this site that you see depicted. Although they found no bodies at the time, they did find evidence of human remains being once been buried there. They found certain artefacts, pieces of clothing, I think some documents, other things indicating that humans had been buried there. From the testimony of witnesses and the evidence in the video, you will see that they were buried as shown in the left half of that image. Later investigations show that on approximately the 1st or 2nd of June, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia had returned to Izbica and removed those bodies from their graves. Serb authorities eventually, in 2001 or 2002, admitted having removed the bodies. To this date, all 120-plus bodies that were there have not been found. About 59 have been discovered, 20 of them were in a clandestine mass grave site near Petrovo Selo, a site called Petrovo Selo 2, which is located in Serbia near -- in eastern Serbia near the border with Romania. Others have been found in various locations in the Kosovska Mitrovica municipality in Kosovo. Once again, you see evidence of an attempt to cover up the crime, suggesting a guilty conscience on the part of the Serb authorities. As in Suva Reka, the Serbs once again had to engage in grave-robbing to hide the evidence. We suggest the only logical inference is that the individuals under authority of our accused dug up those victims and transported them more than 250 kilometres to end up in Petrovo Selo 2. One last killing site I want to talk about before talking about the deportations. We'll talk about Meja, a village in the Djakovica municipality. This was later, on the 27th of April, 1999, in Djakovica municipality, forces of the FRY and Serbia began a large-scale operation an area called the Erenik and Trava River Valleys. On your screen you have a map now. You can see Djakovica identified by a red circle and arrows pointing to the river valley areas for the Erenik River and the Trava River. You also see the Kosovo-Albania border in a pink or purple line on the lower left side. This operation in the river valley areas ended up with Kosovo Albanians fleeing and several convoys being formed. In the vicinity of Meja, forces of the FRY and Serbia detained and separated hundreds of Kosovo Albanian men in those convoys. Several were summarily executed, and another 300 were never seen alive again. Two years later, forensic teams investigating a mass grave site inside the grounds of the barracks of the SAJ, the anti-terrorist police unit, discovered some 344 bodies. DNA identification has determined that 289 of those bodies were the remains of men removed by forces of the FRY and Serbia from the convoys, attempting to flee Meja on the 27th of April, 1999. And again we put up a map to show you the relative distance from Meja to Batajnica, being approximate to the distance from The Hague to Luxembourg. Again of these 300 bodies, approximately 289 removed 280 kilometres to get from Meja to that hole in the ground outside Belgrade. As I said before, a significant logistical challenge, requiring important resources while engaged in an armed conflict with NATO and KLA. Now, before I go on to talk about the deportations, I want to direct your attention to another matter worth noting in regard to the killings. In our indictment we have attached schedules listing the names of those known killed at the killing sites. Based on my rough mathematical calculations, the number of named identified individuals in those schedules totals about 924. Of those 924, 53 of them were children under the age of 16; 72 were females; 104 were over the age of 65 years. We suggest that these are not what you might expect to see from a legitimate campaign against the armed terrorists of the KLA, but rather reflect killings of civilians in a programme to remove them from Kosovo.
