Now I'd like to talk about deportations, and we'll put up a map showing our deportation sites referred to in the indictment. The evidence will show a pattern of conduct by the forces of FRY and Serbia which supports the inference that this was a widespread and systematic attack directed at the civilian Kosovo Albanian population, that it was well planned and coordinated from above, and that its objective - or at least one of its primary objectives - was to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to maintain Serb control over the province. Generally speaking, in the eastern half of Kosovo the forces of FRY and Serbia drove and directed the Kosovo Albanians to the south towards Macedonia. In the western half of the province, the joint VJ and MUP operations tended to drive and direct the civilians towards Albania. I want to talk about some of these individual deportation sites. On the map now you'll see the five of the primary border-crossing points, two for Macedonia and three for Albania marked in purple. These are the primary border-crossing points through which the victims of this operations were funneled out of Kosovo. First of all, I want to talk about Pec. You'll see it marked by the green dot there on the left side. In the city of Pec, Pec municipality, forces of the FRY and Serbia went from house to house forcing Kosovo Albanians to leave their homes. In the course of this process, some civilians were shot and killed and houses were set on fire. Serb soldiers and police directed the civilians to the town centre where those without their own vehicles were forced to get on buses and in trucks. They were then driven to Prizren and towards the border with Albania. The Kosovo Albanians were then forced off the buses and trucks and directed to walk the last 15 kilometres to Albania. And you'll see a little graphic demonstrating the areas to which they went. A few from Pec actually went into Montenegro, but you'll hear evidence that the majority went south to Djakovica and then out to Albania. Once they arrived at the border and before leaving Kosovo, they were ordered to turn over those identity papers to the forces of the FRY and Serbia. Next I would like to talk about Prizren municipality, located in the south and identified by the red dot on your map. Between the 25th and the 28th of March, in the very first week after the NATO bombing began, forces of the FRY and Serbia began attacking villages in this municipality, first in the village of Pirane, and then several others, forcing the Kosovo Albanians from their homes and sending them to the Albanian border. You'll see an image of this deportation. In the town of Prizren itself, beginning on the 28th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia again went from house to house, ordering the Kosovo Albanians to leave. They formed convoys using all available vehicles, with many having to make the 15-kilometre journey to the border on foot. Along the way, some of the Kosovo Albanian men were beaten or killed by forces of the FRY and Serbia. In some cases, women were separated from the convoy and raped. Once at the border, again the Kosovo Albanians had their personal identity documents taken away from them by the Serbs before being allowed or being directed to cross into Albania. Pristina, the capital, we'll put a map up of that. The capital city itself wasn't immune to Serb efforts to remove Kosovo Albanian civilians. Beginning on the 24th of March and for several weeks thereafter, up until late May, forces of the FRY and Serbia went from house to house and forced the Kosovo Albanians to leave. Many of them left immediately to the train station, while others went to other parts of the city, but for the most part those doing so only temporarily delayed their ultimate removal from the town. During the course of these expulsions, a number of the civilians were killed. Several women were sexually assaulted by the forces of FRY and Serbia. Once removed from their homes, they were directed by the Serb police to the train station, where they were packed on to trains or buses. Then they were taken south to a point near the border - Djeneral Jankovic is the name of the town in Serbian, Hani i Elezit in Albanian - where they had to get off the train and then walk the last part or their exodus along the railroad tracks across the border into Macedonia. On their way from Pristina to Macedonia, many had their identity papers taken away from them by forces of the FRY and Serbia. Most of the ethnic Albanian villagers surrounding Pristina town were also subjected to the same treatment by the forces of FRY and Serbia. They were beaten and robbed, some were killed, and then forced from their homes, which were then looted and burned. Many of them also eventually were put on trains heading to Macedonia, and they too had to walk the last stage across the border and out of Kosovo. Some others from Pristina took an alternate route out of Kosovo and ordered to get to Albania, and you'll see that reflected on the screen before you. Finally, the last deportation municipality I want to speak about is Urosevac on the map before you indicated by the pink circle in the south-eastern part of Kosovo. Beginning with the onset of the NATO bombing on the 24th of March, the forces of the FRY and Serbia began shelling and attacking villages in Urosevac municipality in the usual pattern I've described before. The villagers were ordered to leave, their abandoned houses were burned by the Serb forces. Most of the villagers ended up in the town of Urosevac itself, where they boarded trains heading for the border-crossing point near Djeneral Jankovic, and like the others mentioned above from Pristina, walking the last part along the railway line. At the border the forces of FRY and Serbia took their identity documents before they crossed into Macedonia. The indictment, in addition to the killings and deportations, also charges these accused with persecutions, including rapes and the destruction of property. I want to say a few words about that. You will hear testimony from a number of victims about the sexual assaults committed upon them by forces of the FRY and Serbia during these operations to remove the Kosovo Albanian population. I won't go into specific or graphic detail about these horrific crimes now, but only mention that this evidence will be led during our case and that for several of these witnesses we have sought and been granted protective measures. We have also proposed an expert to testify on certain aspects of these crimes and the impact on the victims. We say these rapes were part of the widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population and an integral part of the persecutions and the objective of the JCE. They occurred throughout the province as Kosovo Albanians were terrorised and expelled from Kosovo. Destruction of cultural sites and religious buildings. Another type of crime under the persecutions count includes damage to religious and cultural property. A number of witnesses, including the expert, Andras Reidlmayer, will testify about this. And we've got some photos of that damage to show you. First is a mosque in Bela Crkva, which we've talked about; next is another one in Brestovac; Velika Krusa, also in Orahovac; Djakovica; also from Djakovica; Vucitrn; another one in Vucitrn; and finally another view of a -- one in Vucitrn; and in Celina; and Cirez; and Landovica. This is evidence, we say, not only of the crime itself of the destruction of those buildings, but also as reflecting the intent and the plan of the perpetrators, that is that the Kosovo Albanians would be driven out and without not be coming back. The evidence regarding this damage also shows and refutes the suggestion that it was done by NATO bombing. The evidence will show that these mosques were not damaged from the air, but rather from the ground by forces of the FRY and Serbia. Mosques were burned and damaged throughout Kosovo, as you've seen. Other sites destroyed included the old bazaar and historic old quarter in Djakovica town, the Hadrum mosque, and the Islamic library. The destruction of cultural and religious sites, we say, was an integral part of this campaign of persecutions. Now I'd like to talk briefly about failure to punish or lack of punishment under Article 7(3) of the Statute. The evidence will further show that none of these crimes charged in the indictment were properly investigated, if investigated at all, nor were the perpetrators punished. This general impunity for serious violations of humanitarian law against ethnic Albanians in Kosovo didn't exist because of any problems of the courts not functioning during the conflict; the courts were functioning. Both civilian and military courts worked regularly during the conflict and thereafter. Military courts were attached to the Pristina Corps command, the Pristina Military District, and the 3rd Army command. Nevertheless, we say, impunity prevailed for a certain type of crime, namely the crimes we're dealing with in this trial, crimes committed by Serbs against Kosovo Albanians. In contrast, VJ members were frequently and regularly investigated and punished in proceedings before military courts for certain offences, mainly disciplinary matters, things in the nature of desertion, absence without leave, sleeping on duty, insubordination, but they were never or almost never prosecuted for crimes of deportation, murder, rape, robbery, or destruction and damage committed against ethnic Kosovo Albanians and their property. To illustrate this point, I would like to show you a graphic. As you can see from this chart, more than 90 per cent -- well, let me tell you. This describes the types of criminal offences through June 1999. This was from an exhibit produced by a Defence witness in the Milosevic case. You'll see on the lower left other crimes were 3 per cent, crimes against life and limb were 6 per cent, all the other crimes, 90 per cent, or the failure to respond to call-up, desertion, or insubordination, or other crimes against the VJ. These disciplinary offences, these statistics are based on numbers contained in a Supreme Command Staff document that will come into evidence, we hope, later in the trial. As for these crimes designated as "others," most of those were crimes against property. Most were for robbery or aggravated robbery or theft. 20 per cent were for vehicle thefts. Let me show you a second chart. This one is based on a report of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'll again beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were the properties occupied, those vacated?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't tell you that at this point. That's something that may appear in the report, but I don't have that answer yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This second report, this charge is based on a report of the military court in Nis to the supreme military court in Belgrade. It was reporting on criminal cases heard by the military courts during the Kosovo conflict from 24 March 1999 until 10 June 1999. You can see how low the percentage of cases concerning war crimes against the civilian population is: 1 per cent. On the lower right you'll see the red pie slice. And rape cases are listed as 3 per cent. These statistics clearly suggest, and we expect to prove with other evidence during the trial, that the widespread persecution, deportation, murders, mistreatments, rape, and destruction of property against ethnic Kosovo Albanians was not a matter of serious concern for Serb authorities. There was no meaningful substantive effort to fully investigate such matters, nor to see that VJ and/or MUP perpetrators of such crimes were punished. The occasional rare investigations of serious incidents which did take place were superficial, and the perpetrators remained unknown, unlocated, uncharged, and/or unpunished. The evidence we'll lead on the investigation into the massacre at Izbica as an example of this practice of a token effort, just going through a few motions in effect in order to be able to say to the outside world: Look, we -- see, we tried. We did do something. The impunity for the crimes concerned by this indictment went hand in hand, we say, with the attempts to conceal those crimes. Milosevic, Milutinovic, Sainovic, and others prevented the Prosecutor and investigators of the Tribunal from carrying out investigations in Racak after the killings in January 1999. Even before any domestic investigations were conducted there, Milosevic declared publicly that members of the forces of the FRY and Serbia had not committed any crimes. At different crime scenes described before, the perpetrators attempted to dispose of the corpus delicti, the human remains and bodies of the murdered victims, in some cases by dynamiting the house in which the massacre had taken place, or by hiding the corpses in wells. In other cases you've seen the bodies were removed long distances to be buried in Serbia. We will present evidence about this with regard to the killings in Mala Krusa, Cirez, and Kacanik, among others. The attempt to conceal crimes by disposing the bodies wasn't limited to just these few sites. As we already talked about with regard to Suva Reka, where hundreds of bodies were transferred vast distances across Kosovo and into Serbia and ended up in secret mass graves, the extent of this operation, we say, the organisation and the involvement of Serb officials therein, is best shown by the fact that one of the largest mass graves with more than 300 bodies -- several hundred bodies of ethnic Kosovo Albanians was at the firing range of the spatial anti-terrorist unit, the SAJ, in Batajnica, close to Belgrade. We say senior Serb officials personally administrated this operation. Finally the evidence will show that in many cases crimes committed against ethnic Kosovo Albanians were not only tolerated but were ordered to be committed by superior officers of the direct perpetrators. In the course of this trial, you will hear live testimony from witnesses who experienced this themselves. We say that this evidence will also prove responsibility of the accused under Article 7(3) for superior responsibility. We say that all of the accused had effective control over the perpetrators, that is they had the material ability to prevent or punish the commission of offensives. They had the material ability to enforce discipline among the troops deployed to Kosovo and to effect the prosecution and punishment of perpetrators by virtue of their respective positions, Milutinovic as the president of Serbia; Sainovic as the Deputy Prime Minister and the head of the Joint Command; Ojdanic as the Chief of Staff of the VJ; Pavkovic as the commander of the 3rd Army; and Lazarevic as the head or the commander of the Pristina Corps; and Sreten Lukic as the head of the MUP staff. By virtue of both their de jure and de facto powers, it was within their power and their authority to take measures that would have prevented crimes or punished the perpetrators appropriately. The evidence will also show that all of the accused knew or had reason to know that serious violations of humanitarian law, as described earlier, were committed by the VJ and MUP forces or forces subordinated to them or incorporated into them and working and operating with them in Kosovo. They had general information in their possession which would put them on notice. And they also knew about the criminal activity of and the criminal propensity of certain elements within their troops. Despite their superior positions and their material ability to take necessary measures and their knowledge, they failed to prevent and they failed to punish the crimes. That's why we say they are responsible under Article 7(3). Now, before answering the last of my journalistic questions, the why question, and concluding, I want to make a few remarks about some other general things that will pertain during the trial. We will have a number of insider witnesses testify during this case, a fair number of so-called insiders. Generally these will be Serbs who were members of the VJ or the MUP. They will come, I suggest, with varying degrees of reluctance to testify and you will see their discomfort, which may occur for many reasons. One reason is that many of their fellow countrymen hold the view that any Serb who testifies for the OTP, for the Prosecutor, in a case against Serb accused, such a person is a traitor, to his country and to his fellow Serbs. Others may be concerned about some of their own conduct during the conflict. Not all are going to come before you, I suggest, with clean hands. And they may unreasonably deny or downplay their own roles in the events. Some will be, I suggest, downright hostile to the Prosecution. It would be nice for the Prosecution if all our witnesses were as pure as new-fallen snow, but that's not how it works in real life. I would like to have Mother Theresa and a couple of nuns and some boy scouts to be all of our witnesses, but those aren't the people who are going to be in a position who are going to have inside knowledge of a joint criminal enterprise in a war crimes case. So I want to alert you to that, and we are confident that Your Honours will be able to judge these witnesses, and in cases where it's necessary, to be able to separate the wheat from the chaff and know which parts are wholly true and those that might be something less. And a related matter regarding evidence, you'll see a number of documents in this case, I'm sorry to say, or maybe I should be glad to say, we don't have a complete collection of all the documents produced and created by the Serbian authorities during the conflict, we don't have all the army documents or all of the MUP documents. You've heard from some of the pre-trial proceedings, Mr. President, that even the Defence has had some difficulty in obtaining documents from the MUP. It's an ongoing process, and there can be all kinds of reasons for the delays which we may discuss during the presentation of the case. It's also interesting to note that General Pavkovic was involved in the creation of the VJ Commission on Cooperation with the ICTY. In some ways that seems like having the fox guard the hen-house, but that's something that we have to deal with as a fact of life in this case. Thirdly I want to mention the crime base victims. We had initially proposed several of those witnesses as 92 bis witnesses to come -- to submit their evidence through the written statements and not have them appear, but based on the pre-trial rulings they will be appearing before you. Since they will be coming, it's our proposal to lead some of their evidence on direct because I think, as we discussed last week, Your Honours, we have a concern about having these witnesses come in and have to directly be submitted to cross-examination without having a brief chance to tell in their own words about their experience. And finally I think I also foreshadowed this possibility, that in addition to the team you have before you today, Mr. Stamp, my co-equal, Senior Trial Attorney on this case, Christina Moeller, Mr. Mathias Marcussen, and Patricia Fikirini, Trial Attorneys, we have some other lawyers who will be make appearances in this case during the course of the trial. Now, that takes me to my last journalistic question posed at the beginning, the why question. Why did these crimes happen? As I said, motive is not an element that we have to prove, but I think it will help you understand the evidence and place it in context. We say the short and simple answer is that Kosovo was central to the political survival of Milosevic and his inner circle. Slobodan Milosevic and his fellow participants in this JCE, in this joint criminal enterprise, we say, were sick and tired of the Kosovo problem. Over the preceding eight years, they had seen their Yugoslavia shrink from six republics to two, and they were determined not to yield any more territory, and certainly not Kosovo. As Milosevic told NATO Generals Wesley Clark and Klaus Naumann, Kosovo was worth more than his own head. For years they had tried various measures but without success. The Serbs were losing the demographic game in Kosovo, and it was only going to get worse. You'll see the varying percentages of Albanians as a total -- as a percentage of the total population was going up and that of the Serbs was going down. Efforts to deal with the problem through legislation and increasingly discriminatory measures didn't work either. Use of force by the police and then the military didn't work. Actually, those efforts only made the situation worse. More and more Kosovo Albanians abandoned the notion of non-violent civil resistance, as led by Ibrahim Rugova and the LDK, and they turned to the KLA and a programme of violent resistance. By the time the international community and NATO decided to act, the decision, we say, had been made and the forces put into place to finally make a significant change in the ethnic balance in Kosovo. The NATO campaign gave the JCE members an opportunity to do under the cover of a state of war what they dared not do in peacetime, and that was to drive hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians out of the province and out of the country. In conclusion, Your Honours, and I'm ending much earlier than I anticipated, hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians were forced to flee for their lives, to leave their homes on little or no notice at all, they were driven out by the shelling by the VJ and at gunpoint by the police, the special units and other forces of the FRY and Serbia. Thousands were killed in the process, uncounted numbers were robbed. Men were beaten, women raped. Their homes and businesses they had to leave behind were looted and burned to the ground. Their mosques and cultural and religious buildings were destroyed. We say this was not just collateral damage from a conflict between the KLA and the forces of the FRY and Serbia, nor was it caused by the NATO bombings. It wasn't an accident, and it wasn't a series of coincidences, nor was it simply the sad and difficult consequences of a legitimate anti-terrorist campaign. This was a plan, directed from above, coordinated by these other members of the joint criminal enterprise, using the forces under their command and control to bring about that objective of the JCE, that one I repeated many times before, modifying the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to maintain Serbian control of the province. This is not a case where we have confessions by the accused nor a smoking-gun document setting forth a plan calling for a final solution for the Kosovo problem, but all the evidence considered together in a common sense fashion can only lead to the inference and the solid conclusion that these crimes were part of a common plan or purpose for which these accused and the other named members of the joint criminal enterprise, came together and made their respective contributions with the intention that the objective be achieved, intending or knowing that the crimes would be committed to achieve that goal. There are a few key factors I want to reiterate and ask you to keep in mind during the presentation of evidence in this case. Number one is the nature of the armed campaign beginning on the 24th of March, 1999, the coordinated, widespread, systematic nature of the attacks all across the province beginning on that day; number 2, the number of children, women, and elderly victims, obviously not KLA fighters or terrorists; number 3, the efforts to conceal the crimes, first by denying their occurrence, and then by taking great logistical pains and using precious resources to remove the evidence, such as by digging up the bodies of victims and transporting them hundreds of kilometres to hide them in mass grave sites in Serbia; number 4, the confiscation and destruction of identity documents and vehicle licence plates; number 5, statements of intention by Milosevic and others about the Kosovo Albanians and finding a solution for the problem in the spring of 1999, a solution like the one that Milosevic said was done in 1945 and 1946, getting them together and shooting them all; number 6, the removal of nay-sayers from the inner circles of the leadership and replacement of those with others that were more agreeable, more willing, to go along with what was planned; number 7, the importance of Kosovo to the political rise and survival of Slobodan Milosevic and his supporters. At the end of our case when the evidence is all in, we expect it will show and we will ask you to find all six of these accused guilty as charged. I thank you for the opportunity to have spoken to you this morning, and I and my colleagues look forward to presenting our case to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we're minded to take the break early and resume at quarter to 2.00 so that Mr. Ojdanic can give his statement uninterrupted, since you envisage it being concluded well within the period of one session. Does that meet with your approval or would you rather he started now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. What we'll do now is adjourn until 1.45. We'll resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.09 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ojdanic, you may now make the statement your counsel indicated that you would be making at this point. Just stand up and let us hear what you have to say. THE ACCUSED OJDANIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, standing in front of you as a soldier, a four-star general, my honourable professional career spans over 42 years. Back in 1964, I took an oath to serve my people and my country. I solemnly undertook to faithfully serve my people, to defend my home country, and to always be prepared to fight for the freedom and honour of my country, without sparing my own life, if need be. We all carry a debt to our home country, whereas our home country owes no one anything. I taught everybody the same thing, my officers in my commands at times when I was the leader of tactical operations and strategic commands. I taught all the future officers of our army the same thing at the time when I served as a lecturer and head at the military academy of the land forces of the JNA. The defence of the home country is our supreme value. It taught me the following, and this is what I tried to each everybody else: There is no shying away from danger or fear. Thank you very much for allowing me to take the floor at the very beginning of this trial. I've been waiting for seven years to remove this feeling of shame. I felt the need to address you at the beginning of this trial in order to introduce myself, not just as a general but also as a human being. I was born on the 1st of June, 1941, in the village of Ravni, near Uzice in Serbia, in a country which at the time was called the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. I was born a mere 56 days after the beginning of the fascist Germany aggression against Serbia. They were joined in this aggression by Hungary and Italy. I was 6 months old when the glorious Uzice republic was established which was the only free territory at the very heart of occupied Europe. I was only 4 years old when the country was liberated from German occupation. As a child, I dreamt of one day becoming a soldier. Both my grandfathers were in the liberating armies in the First World War. My father was an anti-fascist. He took part in the struggle against fascism, chauvinism and anti-Semitism, in which Serbia proudly took part, along with Great Britain, France, the United States of America, and the Soviet Union. I was quite familiar with the involvement of my countrymen in the wars of liberation against Turkey, Austria, and Hungary. My soldierly orientation was based on my knowledge of the famous Uzice army and the 4th Regiment of Stefan Nemanja from the famous Drina Division. As a child, I did not stop at the local level. I read books on our national history. I admired the recognition awarded to the Serbian army and its commanders by the allied powers and the enemy alike. Liote [phoen], the French marshal, wrote: "By their courage, by their resistance, and by their spirit of sacrifice during the war between 1914 and 1918, the Serbian army, under the commander of Prince Regent Aleksandar, provided a shining example of soldierly virtue." Robert Lessin [phoen], the American foreign minister, said: "When history is written, the most illustrious chapter of that history will be named Serbia." The Serbian army created a miracle of fortitude while the Serbian people suffered like no one else. Such perseverance and such sacrifice cannot go unobserved. Indeed, they must be rewarded. There were countless examples of this kind. It filled my soul with a great desire to become a proud Serbian soldier, Serbian soldier who has never covered himself in shame throughout the entire history. At the time, a JNA officer was the most highly respected profession back where I come from. It is, therefore, no surprise that at the age of 15 I ceased being a child and became a soldier. I served for four years in schools and for a further ten years in military academies. I completed the school for junior officers, the military academy, the command staff academy, the operations school, which was also called the All People's Defence school, and I completed a degree in strategy, after which I defended my thesis and earned myself the right to be called a master of military sciences. I gave up the defence of my PhD thesis under strange circumstances. I was an excellent student all the time. I had five fast-track promotions. I was decorated eight times, seven times by the JNA, and once by the Russian army. I was taught that Yugoslavia was a country that must ensure equal rights for all its peoples, a life worth living, and a happy future. I believed in this as the supreme value, which guaranteed that our peoples would never again wage wars among themselves. I was a soldier who was prepared to do everything in my power to strengthen the position of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. I not only believed in brotherhood and unity. I did everything within my power to strengthen it day by day. My duties allowed me to take an active part in the struggle for the equal rights of all the different nations that made up Yugoslavia. My best friends among the officers were and remain members of other ethnic groups than myself. I spent many years in the military academy of the JNA where I worked as a commander, as a teacher, as head of one of the biggest groups of cadets, and as head of one particular department. I trained future officers from all the different ethnic groups inhabiting Yugoslavia. As a JNA officer, I came to Kosovo and Metohija first as a lieutenant-colonel and later on -- first as a second lieutenant and then as a lieutenant-colonel. I served in Djakovica between 1964 and 1965 and in the Prizren garrison between 1983 and 1988. I emphasise that I was there with my family. I also served in the Pristina garrison between 1988 and 1990. I personally saw how the relations between the Serbs and the Albanians were deteriorating. I never, for a moment, believed that I should take sides. I did everything to remove the cause or whatever it was that was bringing about this deterioration in inter-ethnic relations. Common people, both Serbs and Albanians, still respected the JNA at the time. I personally saw what this respect meant among the Albanians in as far as it applied to my own brigade in Prizren. Elements from our brigade built a road through an Albanian village. The way they treated the soldiers was more than just friendly. They did not allow the soldiers to sleep in tents, welcoming them instead in their own homes, which is probably a unique example of hospitality. I felt happy and I felt proud of this. I believed that this stood for growing confidence in the country's institutions. I had a mild optimism in me when I thought about the future and the co-existence of the different ethnic groups in Kosovo. After Kosovo and Metohija, my service brought me back to the General Staff of the JNA, where I served for a while as the chief operative of the land forces and as deputy head of the administration for training and education of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Army of the Republic of Yugoslavia back in 1990 and 1991. Late in 1991, I was the standing commander of the 37th Corps. In 1992 and 1993, I was the commander of the Uzice Corps. I continued to serve in the Belgrade garrison as the army's Chief of Staff. Between 1993 and 1994, and between 1994 and 1996, I was commander of the 1st Army, the greatest strategic unit or group in the entire Yugoslav army. On the 1st of July, 1996, I was appointed deputy Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav army and I remained in that position until the 27th of November, 1998. At this time, which was the hardest of times, I was then appointed the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav army and remained in this position for a mere 14 months. It was between the 15th of -- the 27th of November, 1998 until the 15th of February, 2000. Between February 2000 and the time I submitted a request to retire, I was the federal minister of defence. I left active service as a military officer on the 31st of March, 2001. While talking about my career and where it took me, it is not exaggerated to say that I am one of the few officers who did not skip a single command level in their entire career, starting with squad level and then working my way all the way up to the top of the army and the General Staff. It's very difficult to find the right words in this brief address to express what I feel about the whole thing, what I feel about everything that I am being charged with here, as well as the rest of us, by this indictment. Anything that I may say now, Your Honours, to you or to all those watching or listening I say with a clear and peaceful conscience. I can look everyone in the eye without, for a second, flinching, even bearing in mind the substance of the opening statement of the OTP and in fact despite that opening statement. This has a calming effect on me, this knowledge that I can face anyone, although for the last seven years I have been toiling under those unjustified charges, charges that could only be brought against a human being with no morality, honour, conscience, or human dignity. These charges can never be brought against a man with such an honourable military career behind him. I face you of my own free will. I decided to do so immediately after the Law on Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was adopted by the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I believe that this was the only venue for me to prove my innocence and to prove the truth, given that I can't do this in my own country, which I had served to defend in an honourable and soldierly way. The motto of my life is truth and nothing but the truth, even should truth be harmful to me. As a military officer throughout my career, I complied strictly with all the laws and regulations. Is it possible to imagine at all that I, as the Chief of the General Staff might err in performing my highest constitutional duty? Article 63 of the constitution of the SFRY says, and I quote: "The defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is the right and duty of every citizen." Article 133 of the constitution clearly defines the role and duties of the Yugoslav army. I quote: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has an army, the duty of which it is to defend its sovereignty, its territory, its independence, and its constitutional order." These were also my tasks as Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. Who could defy these provisions of the constitution? Who would have the right? In October 1998, the Supreme Council - and that was before I became Chief of the General Staff - debated the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and arrived at the following conclusion: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would do everything in its power for the situation in Kosovo and Metohija to be resolved in a peaceful way by police work and diplomacy. Should it, however, fail in this, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will be defended by all means at our disposal. This in itself indicated the task of the Yugoslav army and the entire defence system of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The army and my family taught me another rule that I hold sacred. All men, regardless of their skin colour, their ethnicity, or their religion, are equal and must be treated without prejudice or discrimination. I stood by that principle throughout my whole life. It never even crossed my mind to act in a discriminatory way to anyone at all, and I certainly never did anything like that. And this applied to my enemy in armed conflict, whoever this happened to be. The greatest success in my military career occurred in a community that was not populated by my fellow countrymen or they did not constitute a majority. This was of all places in Kosovo and Metohija, more specifically in Prizren. I was the brigade commander there, and the area of responsibility of this brigade covered the whole of Kosovo and Metohija. I was elected as the best commander of the joint tactical units in the JNA and I was awarded the highest possible honour, the award that we refer to as the 22nd December award. Most of the duties in that brigade were performed by Albanian officers, who greatly contributed to the combat-readiness of our brigade. How on earth could I possibly have been selected as the best commander in the entire JNA had I not enjoyed daily support from all my officers and from a great many people from the local community which was predominantly Albanian? If that is true - and trust me, it is - how could I be a great believer in brotherhood and unity? How could I believe in equal rights for all the different ethnic groups, including the Albanian ethnic group? How could I as a man and soldier of the highest rank possibly change overnight and decide to join some sort of joint criminal enterprise and choose to be involved in the planning of the most heinous crimes, the killing and expulsion of people from their own homes in their own country? No, Your Honours. Something doesn't quite tally. Either it is a lie that I was the best commander in an environment that was almost purely Albanian, either it was a lie that I was loved and respected by that community, or it is a lie that I aided, abetted, and instigated the most heinous crime imaginable against those very people. I assure you, the latter is a lie. I never did anything nor did I ever tolerate anything that would even remotely resemble the allegations made in the indictment. Quite the contrary, in fact. You will see countless orders that I gave, countless warnings that I issued, which indicate precisely the opposite. In these clashes in Kosovo and Metohija, it was very difficult to distinguish the front line from the rear, war from politics, struggle from ideology, civilian from soldier. I wrote down in my own hand and I spoke in my own voice. I didn't use a spokesperson, a PR person, or a scribe. Countless pages of orders and warnings to act humanely under these difficult and inhumane circumstances that prevailed in a war, all with the objective of avoiding unnecessary suffering to the civilians. And we know that civilians are always the greatest and saddest casualty of any war. Unfortunately, I was not entirely successful, but one only learned about this later on, if that is even true. However, I remain convinced that by my acts, by my word, and by my personal authority, I contributed to keep this down, to keep the extent of the whole thing down. I also remain convinced that none of my acts, written or spoken, were never used by anyone as an instigation to commit or perpetrate possible crimes against the Albanian population. I remain particularly convinced that at no time in my very long and very successful military career did I do anything that might qualify as a crime or any form of participation in a crime. It therefore follows that I certainly didn't do that as the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. I was a firm believer in international law and in the UN Charter. I hoped that the UN -- that NATO would never attack my country, although everything was indicating the opposite, namely that there would be an aggression. This optimism, then as of now, was founded on a belief that there was no international problem that could be resolved by the use of force, especially by the use of weapons. I sent a letter to General Clark to express this belief. Unfortunately, General Clark did not share my beliefs, and he was then the chief commander of NATO for Europe. Your Honours, the year now is 2006. It's been seven years since the events described in the indictment. One thing that I would like to ask you, Your Honours, is to try to put yourself in my shoes and imagine how these events unfolded between March and June 1999. Even in official US documents, one comes across references to the Kosovo Liberation Army as a terrorist organisation who were perpetually brutally attacking the Serbian police and the Serbian army, as well as both Albanian and Serb civilians. In peril with this struggle against terrorism, we tried to resist the NATO aggression. The mightiest armies of the world joined in attacking Yugoslavia. This operation was a violation of the provisions of international law, and it was an operation that the Security Council never sanctioned. I personally believe that regardless of what the OTP may or may not say, it won't be possible to use this Kosovo tragedy, the tragedy of all the people living there, to remove the horrible consequences of daily bombings of Yugoslavia and the countless civilian victims that fell in indiscriminate attacks against my own country, which peaked in Kosovo and Metohija. The partnership between NATO and the Kosovo Liberation Army is a fact openly discussed today. The crimes committed at the time were never subjected to the scrutiny of the OTP. If they had, I believe it would be easier for us to arrive at the reasons which drove the Kosovo people to leave their homes. Evidence will show that everything I did was against the Kosovo Liberation Army, and then later after the aggression against my country, against NATO, and the Kosovo Liberation Army as NATO's allies, and not the Albanian -- the civilian population, as is claimed. There is one thing that I am certain about, Your Honours. I am not guilty under any of the counts of the indictment. I face this indictment with a clear conscience because I am blameless. In 2001, already as an accused, I asked the supreme military prosecutor to be tried by a domestic court. Having failed in this and after the Law on Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was adopted, I went to The Hague of my own free will. I believe that Judge Bonomy will remember that at the time, in a bid to prove my innocence, I begged my counsel to ask from NATO to deliver any intercept with me in it or any other document proving my guilt. I could do this because I am certain that I have nothing to hide, I have nothing to be ashamed of, I have nothing to fear, morally or in a purely professional sense. I performed my duties as Chief of Staff of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army or in wartime as the Chief of Staff of the general command in an honourable way. I exhort the OTP to show us intercepts or any other documents or any other evidence which proves that I have an anti-Albanian bias or which proves that I, in any way, instigated or abetted the expulsion of Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija. I was a soldier and I remain one. I always acted upon orders, orders based on law. I always acted upon my own conscience, although I was appointed as Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army at a time when the decision on the aggression had already been adopted, I am still proud of the general command staff, which I headed. I am proud of the Yugoslav army and their commanding officers, because they stood up and resisted an immeasurably superior force within the limits of what was reasonably possible, all the way until the Resolution 1244 was passed and then a withdrawal was ordered. We did not bring shame to our glorious ancestors. We did not, as some ill-informed people seem to suggest, capitulate. How did the Yugoslav army leave Kosovo and Metohija? General Jackson probably provided the best illustration of this. What he said at the time was it was obvious that this was an undefeated and still operational army. For the JNA and its command officers, this is high recognition indeed. After three months of war, after 13 of our tanks were destroyed or damaged, and three -- with 350 fighters defending their home country involved, this was an admirable act. In my heart it is, and I am certain that it applies to all the rest. There is this festering wound and sorrow for all those who killed the police and army alike, as well as the civilians that perished, those belonging to the various ethnic groups, whose sacrifice we still admire. I only wish to offer a couple of elementary conclusions, which I believe will be proven throughout this trial. First of all, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command was a position in which I performed my duties to the best of my ability. I complied with the constitution and with my country's laws, with the laws and customs of war, with the international humanitarian law of war, with the combat rules and the use of units in armed warfare and all the other provisions and regulations. Secondly, there was no plan for the expulsion of Albanians, nor was I involved in any situation where such a plan was discussed. Had this plan indeed existed and had it been openly debated, I would have opposed it; that much is certain. Thirdly, there was no such thing as joint criminal enterprise; therefore, I could not have been involved in one. Fourthly, I never aided or abetted, instigated, or ordered any violations of humanitarian law. Quite the contrary, in fact. Fifthly, I took countless precautions through my command system in order to reduce to the greatest possible degree the possibility of any action that could lead to crimes, especially war crimes. This is certainly not something I would have done as a member of anything resembling a joint criminal enterprise. Sixthly, as for the violations of the humanitarian law of war, those were reported by officers in charge in areas wherever this happened. These people were immediately prosecuted in these very complex circumstances because there was a war on, but measures were taken against these people, appropriate measures, if I may say. I would like to take this opportunity to address the Prosecutor, since we have not had an opportunity to communicate yet. I believe that having heard my opening statement and in view of all the evidence so far and the evidence that will be presented by my Defence team, including a number of credible witnesses and expert witnesses, the Prosecutor will, no doubt, gain a more faithful picture of what happened in the war itself, causing them to give up the charges, to drop the charges, in the indictment and give up all their allegations. That would be a great contribution, not only to this trial but to justice as a whole. Your Honours, I believe that after my Defence case you will have learned that my words are true. You will have learned that I am blameless and innocent, and you will be in a position to rule accordingly and to acquit me. I, once again, wish to thank again for giving me a chance to say this. Thank you very much. I'm sorry if I was reading too quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ojdanic. Please be seated. Now, Mr. Stamp, would you care to call your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I would. Thank you very much and good afternoon. The first witness is Sandra Mitchell. Before she is brought into court, may I just indicate that she is one witness that I am applying that a part -- a major part of her testimony be received pursuant to 89(F), and I would also ask to put a few questions to her. She was originally scheduled for four hours in chief. I will not be taking any significant part of that time, as originally scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the statement you intend to provide simply this one page statement which I have received?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The statement which I intend to submit to the Court is composed of three separate statements, including a -- including two one-page addenda, one done on Saturday, I suspect that is the one that is -- possession of, and two others done in 2002. The others done in 2002 would have been part of the original package which was made available to the parties in the matter some time ago. I think the statement of the 8th of July is P2225, and the statements of 2002 are in P2226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the issue at the moment is a very simple issue of whether this witness should be permitted to give evidence orally but adopting into her evidence written statements. There are three of these. One is the substantive statement and the other two are addenda, as has been explained. I think Mr. Stamp's approaching the matter in this way because Rule 89(F) has within it words which suggest it may be necessary for the Trial Chamber to take a positive decision to admit evidence on basis of the interests of the justice allowing that. Does any Defence counsel have any submission to make that the interests of justice dictate that she should not be allowed to give evidence following that course? All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have prepared and filed a motion in limine seeking to bar introduction through this witness of evidence that comes from the so-called Kosovo/Kosova: As Seen, As Told report prepared by the OSCE based upon several grounds, and to the extent that her written statements do make reference to that report or relate to the matters contained therein, we would have an objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That, I think, is a separate question from the one that I am asking you to deal with at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the question of principle, whether any part of her evidence may be incorporated by her from a written document, leaving aside the question of which parts of that may be objectionable, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As long as it is qualified in proper evidence, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, it seems to me that it shouldn't be necessary to make a separate application in terms of Rule 89(F) every time. If a witness is coming here to say -- to be available for cross-examination and to -- having taken the solemn declaration, to say that a written statement is entirely -- an entirely accurate account, then I can't see any reason in the interests of justice, in general, why that shouldn't happen. Now, that doesn't rule out the possibility of such a situation arising. So the course we will follow from now on is that such witnesses will automatically be entitled to be led in that way, subject to any preliminary objection being taken by the Defence. And it will be for the Defence to take exception; otherwise we will simply accept that the evidence should proceed that way. On the matter raised by Mr. Ivetic, I haven't seen that motion. If it's been filed, then it hasn't reached me yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was only submitted during the pause, the last break that we had, so it is possible it has not made it to the parties yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, I don't know whether it necessarily arises just at the moment. I leave it to anyone who wishes to object to any part of this witness's evidence to take exception to a question that counsel believes will lead to an inadmissible answer or, alternatively, to object to a line of evidence when it's plain what the line of evidence the Prosecutor proposes is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the latest statement that we received from the Office of the Prosecutor lists this report that we take question with, Exhibit P473, as a document which it seeks to submit pursuant to 89(F) as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's wait until we get to the stage of the witness being presented with that particular document, and then we'll address the problem at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you bring in Ms. Mitchell, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you stand up, please, Ms. Mitchell. Now, make yourself comfortable with the equipment, first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then when you feel comfortable, would you take the solemn declaration and read it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you please start by stating your full name?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sandra Lynn Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I am currently the director for the Office of Communities, Returns and Minorities for the United Nations Mission in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And by profession you're a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us about your career as a lawyer involved in human rights and international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's a big question. I have about 12 years' experience working in the Balkans in the conflicts of Bosnia, Kosovo, Macedonia, as well as other similar types of events in Africa and in Asia, both conflict -- working during the actual conflicts, either in a humanitarian operation or in a human rights capacity as well as in post-conflict situations with institution buildings along various topics of the rule of law and human rights institution building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where were you posted or what is your position in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly requested to speak into the microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I wasn't being heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were you posted between October 1998 and April 2000?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I was the director for human rights for the Kosovo Verification Mission in Pristina, and then in the refugee camps in Macedonia and Albania during the NATO air campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to your work at that time as director for human rights in the Kosovo Verification Mission, did you give to the OTP three statements which you have signed, two in the year 2000 and one last Saturday?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you recently review those statements and are the contents of those statements true to the best of your knowledge, in the sense that if you're asked about these issues today, right now, would your answers remain the same?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The statements, Your Honours, as indicated, are P225 [sic] and 226 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the role of the KVM in Kosovo in that period, its creation and mandate.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: There were pre-existing international standards applying to the KVM mission even before it was established, and then there were two specific Kosovo-related international instruments regarding the mandate. The pre-existing legislation and standards concerned the OSCE itself, which is the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, an inter-governmental organisation made up of 55 countries, including at the time the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, although it had suspended status for part of the period. The OSCE, as being made up of these 55 countries, all of whom have signed on to the United Nations declaration for human rights, the international covenant on civil political rights, et cetera, most of the international instruments, and the laws on war, the Geneva Conventions, and the laws of The Hague. So these apply to any OSCE field operation that's deployed, and they had been deploying missions throughout the Balkans since the Dayton Agreement, central Asia, et cetera. The Kosovo-specific governing documents were the United Nations Security Council 1199, which was enacted in September 1998 as a result of escalating displacement of Kosovo civilians. At that time the numbers were in the 2 to 300.000 refugees that were putting tremendous burdens on the surrounding countries. So the Security Council resolution was passed. The resolution provided -- stated that Kosovo at that time was in a state of conflict and provided jurisdiction for this Tribunal as well as urging the parties to allow the return of all the refugees, try to find a peaceful resolution, et cetera. The following month, in October 1998, the head of the OSCE called the chairman in office, of these 55 countries, the chairmanship rotates every year and it's the foreign minister of the particular country that holds the particular the seat. At the time that was the Polish foreign minister Geremek. Foreign Minister Geremek signed an agreement with the foreign minister of Yugoslavia, Jovanovic, which established the Kosovo Verification Mission between the governing authorities in Serbia at the time and the OSCE. And that mandate brought in 1199 and provided for regular reporting to Yugoslav officials and other specific things and was the basis in which the mission was stood up. It put a cap of 2.000 staff members, which was met very rapidly. And in a period of about 90 days, the OSCE set up a field operation that contained a headquarters in Pristina, five regional offices in more than 40 other smaller presences throughout Kosovo, where there were tensions and conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just say for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask a question arising out of that. That exercise took beyond the end of 1998, just the setting up exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Security Council resolution in September, the agreement with the FRY or Yugoslav authorities in October, the immediate plans and preparation, deployment of a team to Vienna to stand up this mission, the OSCE had never done a mission of this size before. One hadn't been seen like this since UNPROFOR in Bosnia. Between November and December, the staffing started at a very robust rate by all member countries. And by the time of the withdrawal of the mission, there were more than -- and the mission withdrew in March of 1999, there was more than 1.300 international staff and several thousand national staff employed at the mission at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reason I asked the question is just to gauge how much the activity of the personnel may have been concentrated on simply setting up the mission throughout the period before the bombing actually started, and it seems to me it may have been a substantial part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the most remarkable build-up of a mission that I've been involved in. The funding was incredible, largely through governments like Norway that were going to be moving in to leading the OSCE in 1999, several hundred million dollars, resources were poured in. This was a serious peacekeeping operation to stop, at the time, the flow of refugees. So the logistical side was really impressive of a scale -- like I've said, I've not seen, and in large part because countries utilised all their own resources in telecommunications, transportations, getting resources in theatre very quickly, and OSCE has much, much faster administrative procedures than the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told it's important these numbers are properly reflected on the record. So may I just indicate that at page 83, lines 15, 16, it should be P2225 and P2226. I think on the record the numbers were not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Mitchell, bearing in mind that the role of the human rights division of the KVM is discussed in the statements you have given to us and which we're apprised of, can you briefly tell us what was the primary role of the mission of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: The primary role for the human rights division was to verify the observance of human rights in Kosovo by authorities, both the governing authorities, the VJ, the Yugoslav army, the Serbian police, the special forces, the UCK, the Kosovo Liberation Army, anyone that was exerting any type of control over the civilian population. The second part of the mandate was to coordinate and cooperate. Primarily my department's responsibilities were with the International Committee of the Red Cross on detentions and missing persons, UN High Commissioner for Refugees on displacement, and the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal for evidence and of crimes that were being committed while we were in theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind that much of this is already documented, could you tell us if you published any major document and the sources and methodology of this document as prepared?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: The KVM produced a large volume of documents. The human rights division had pretty clear methodologies in place. It's difficult for me to answer that question without trying to put a little bit of context into the environment that we were operating under at the time. Because it -- the methodology did tend to change when we were in Kosovo and when we were dealing with refugee statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Among the documents that appeared one was entitled was As Seen, As Told.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: As Seen, As Told, Part I, there's are two parts to that report, was the culmination of all the human rights documentation processes and procedures that we undertook in Kosovo from October until March. All of the human rights files were evacuated with the mission, and I can go into the methodology further, if you want, and then the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, could you just tell us briefly first. As Seen, As Told, Part 1, was a report on what?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That was a report of the human rights violations and humanitarian law violations --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- be seated just for a moment. Complete your answer, please, Ms. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that were documented by the human rights officers of the mission between the period October 1998 to June 1999 and also included statements that were collected from thousands of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the objection that's being taken to this evidence is to the admission of it. And it may be, Mr. Ivetic, that the Trial Chamber has to hear a bit more about the methodology and then perhaps see even examples from the material itself before it can make a proper determination upon your objection. The fact that we do that doesn't mean that the material has been admitted, because this is material which will have to be -- on which a positive decision to admit it will have to be taken in light of the fact that you have taken objection to it. But do you really see us being in a position to deal with it adequately before we have heard the methodology that was used to compile it and the general nature of the material contained in the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I thought that it might be useful for the Court to have in mind the specific types of objections that we have so that while considering the testimony as to the methodology of the report you can bear that in mind and perhaps facilitate the process of reaching a decision as to the propriety of that type of testimony or evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear that. I think, Ms. Mitchell, in the circumstances since we're almost at the time for a break, the best thing is for you to leave the courtroom just now. We will be resuming no earlier than 3.15, and depending on how long I listen to Mr. Ivetic just now, it might be slightly later than that. But as long as you're ready to resume at 3.15, that's adequate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have copies of your motion for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have unsigned copies, Your Honour, that I could distribute to both the OTP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you pass them to us then, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm wondering if one of those copies could also been able to us. We have not been able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was going to provide a copy for counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, speaking for myself, the only thing set out here on which I need some elaboration is paragraph -- where are we. In paragraph 3 on the first page, it says that the information collected not only is hearsay but neither follows nor complies with the manner, that means -- I think the word is prescribed by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal for the admission of evidence. Now, what rules are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, essentially it's our position that this report and the testimony of Ms. Mitchell arising from it attempts to introduce into evidence by written form the statements of unnamed alleged victims that are unknown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I followed -- I've read all that. I'd like you to direct me to the rule that you say is being breached by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe if the statements of the witnesses of the alleged occurrences are being submitted written form, they need to comply with Rule 92(F) -- I apologise, 92 bis, Your Honour. So in that sense we believe that the witness who has already testified that a portion of her staff's work was to conduct investigative work for the ICTY, which I submit means the Office of the Prosecutor, trying to get this unsworn anonymous unverifiable testimony in written form through her is trying to get inadmissible testimony in through the backdoor, which we would take grave objection to. And essentially, as Your Honours have already heard, the witness has qualified the report as being conclusions of laws that were breached. In essence, the report seeks to supplant the role of the Trial Chamber in viewing facts and making factual and legal determinations based upon those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these are different -- I understand all the submissions you've made; that's not the question I'm asking you. I'm just trying to identify the rule you say which is being breached, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say it's Rule 89(F) which is being breached by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 92 bis, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Insofar as the report purports to contain written statements of actual eye-witnesses to occurrences and that report is being submitted in written form, I believe the testimony would have to be sworn and in the proper format to be submitted into evidence in that manner. Trying to do so by way of this report and by way of this witness appears to me to be a way around the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your way of characterising the issues to say that each of the persons from whom information has been gathered is a witness and therefore subject to the rule. So it's a question of how the Trial Chamber interprets the word "witness."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we may be assisted in interpreting the word "witness" by looking also at the practice that's been followed so far in the Tribunal and by looking at Rule 89(C), which says: "The Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, so long as the probative value is not outweighed by the prejudicial effect. And as the motion sets forth, given that the source material for these statements, including the identities of alleged victims and alleged perpetrators are not included in the report, were not ever disclosed to the Defence, makes it impossible to seek to rebut this testimony, and therefore I submit the prejudicial effect to all of the accused, really, is quite severe indeed, particularly in light of the fact that the report itself questions the -- I should say admits that there are questions as to the veracity of some of the statements insofar as there were inconsistencies between different interviewees about different incidents and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need you to repeat more or less word for word what I've already read. Don't you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you want to add something to what you've written, then please do that, but all you're doing is repeating what you've already set out in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I stand on those written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We join in the motion that my colleague, Mr. Ivetic, has filed, and obviously, Your Honour, under 82(C) can admit the report if you're satisfied with its reliability. For traditionally admitted hearsay, whether they are satisfied of the reliability of the document. We question the reliability of this document, its objectivity, and, Your Honour, if the Trial Chamber would permit, there's a procedure that's used very frequently in the United States. It's called the voir dire examination, and in this case I think it would take five minutes or less. Just very brief questions to Ms. Mitchell to assist Your Honours in deciding whether this is the kind of document that should be admitted in evidence. Now I would withdraw that request if Your Honour, just on the face of things, decided it's not admissible. But if you do have doubt or if you think it would assist you at all, I would ask for permission to speak very briefly during the -- just interrupt the direct examination for a few minutes to ask some questions which show, in our view, why this report is unreliable and should not be accepted by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We adopt and support the Lukic submission, and one point. And I would direct the Trial Chamber to Rule 95, which states that: "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical, to and would seriously damage, the integrity of the proceedings." Your Honour, I think weighting in all circumstances against Rule 89(C) that the prejudice outweighs the -- any value that these statements may have and are, therefore, inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. With your leave, Your Honour, unfortunately I don't know what it says in my learned friend's submission. However, what I have heard in the oral submissions I would like to say that we accept. I would just like to draw your attention to two things. First of all is the fact that the document that we are now discussing does not have the level of reliability that would suffice for acceptance. None of the sources quoted in the document are named. Some people are mentioned, some women, some statements. None of that is named, does not have a name. And when we -- if we don't have that, we do not have the opportunity to verify the reliability of the documents or statements given by those people. The fact that I've just mentioned leads to another fact, and that is that this document does not have the sufficient level of reliability to be accepted. Having read a statement by Mrs. Mitchell, we have learned that all of these documents have been handed over to the Prosecution of the Tribunal in 2002 when this statement was first taken. As far as I know, these statements have never been disclosed to the Defence teams. I would also like to draw your attention to a decision from the Strugar case dating 26th of May, 2004. In this decision, the matter that was tackled is very similar. I'll give you the exact name of the decision. [In English] "Of certain documents" -- [Interpretation] This was in Strugar case on 26th of May, 2004, following a debate between the parties on the inadmissibility of a piece of evidence marked as MFI 51, which contained a number of statements that were obtained in a similar way as the statements dealt with by OSCE that are being introduced through Ms. Mitchell. And the Trial Chamber rejected that document, that compilation of unnamed sources or documents, due to the fact that there was not a sufficient level of reliability of the document, and also for the fact that the documents were not marked, that the statements of these people did not have the source, it was not known who took the statements, under what circumstances, and that is why the Trial Chamber in this case decided not to admit this document that is very similar to the document that is being introduced at the moment through Ms. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the Defence of General Lazarevic would like to join the submission by the Lukic team and everything that has been said to far. I would like to add to that that in the statement that's given by Ms. Mitchell there are some things that will have an impact on the reliability of those statements. When those statements were taken, one had to take into account the objectivity, the training of the person who took the statements, and we do not know who took the statements, what persons took the statements, whether they were objective and trained to do that. This is what you can find in Ms. Mitchell's statements, and this is an additional argument for which we would like to join whatever has been said so far by our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Well, it is time for us to break. We'll resume at half past 3.00 and give an indication then of how this should be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I hope, I think Your Honour will no doubt give me an opportunity to respond before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It may not just be an opportunity to respond; it may be an opportunity to expand in some way to explain the position further to us, but we need to give consideration to these submissions first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we've decided to do is hear this evidence under reservation of its admissibility. Now, that means that all issues of cross-examination will require to be explored before we decide whether the evidence is admissible. It satisfies the point made by Mr. Sepenuk and allows any issues relating to its reliability and authenticity. Similarly, it deals with the point made by Mr. O'Sullivan, founding on Rule 95. But the Chamber feels that it will be best enabled to make a final decision on admissibility in the light of all the information it can obtain from examination and cross-examination. Once we have heard the evidence in its entirety, we'll make a decision . It may not be an immediate decision but it will be made very shortly after the evidence has been completed. It's not a question of holding this decision over until much later in the trial process. So we should have -- we should have Ms. Mitchell back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But before we proceed, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's one thing I should say for the record. One of the complaints was that these are ordinary persons giving statements that are not available to the Defence.
