I think I should put this on the record and make it quite clear before the end of the cross-examination that these statements are available, and it is the responsibility of the Defence when they receive the -- when they receive the statement of Sandra Mitchell in which she says that she gave these statements, underlying statements, that the report is based on to the ICTY to make that request, there are specific rule, Rule 66(B), that request has not been made so far as I know. So that is not a complaint, I think, to be raised here and I would not want at the end of cross-examination an issue as to these underlying statements to arise without that being made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the point that was being made was that these statements hadn't been disclosed, as you acknowledge, and what you're now confirming is they weren't disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, they were not. The rules of disclosure in the Tribunal are pretty straightforward, although there is a lot of debate in regard to them. But I think they are pretty straightforward. These rules do not fall under -- these underlying statements, except for about 12, do not fall under Rule 66(A), neither do they fall under Rule 68. As a matter of fact, they are the opposite of Rule 68. They are highly inculpatory. The Defence, having been notified a long time ago that this witness would testify for the Prosecution, that this document would be a part of the exhibits for the Prosecution, that these are the underlying documents that support this publication, would have been due to -- it's my submission, to make the request to see these documents under Rule 66(B) which provides for that long before she comes to testify. So I would not want at the end of the cross-examination to hear that there is a Rule 66(B) request for these documents. There are other matters which I think could be addressed, but I believe, as -- that it is quite correct and I accept the decision of Your Honour that the ruling in respect of admissibility should be made after the foundation of evidence is heard. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will hear everyone's submissions at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I think in light of Mr. Stamp's comment, I think I really do have to make one comment. Again, I got in this case a bit late, but when I got in I found out through the other Defence lawyers that none of these refugee interrogation forms, one question of which is your reasons for leaving Kosovo, which is one of the pivotal issues in this case, had not been disclosed. So at the Status Conference last week I asked Mr. Hannis and Mr. Stamp if they had copies of these statements. The answer was yes. And I said I would certainly like you to turn over copies and certainly to the extent they are exculpatory, please do so and certainly as to witnesses who are gaining to testify, could we have those copies for cross-examination. So just to correct the record in that respect, a specific request was made last week of both Mr. Hannis and Mr. Stamp in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a qualified request, Mr. Sepenuk, on the terms in which you've just explained it. If you're looking for copies of all the underlying material, then perhaps that's what you should have asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact, Your Honour, I did, but I said I didn't think that I was justified in asking for all the material except to the extent that it was exculpatory. And if it was not exculpatory, and that of course would be in the decision of the Prosecution team, I said at the very least could you turn over the statements, those statements, for the witnesses who are definitely going to be here so we can use it on cross-examination. Both Mr. Hannis and Mr. Stamp did answer that in the affirmative and said that when those -- before those witnesses testify we can have a copy of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I suspect the answer is that none of it's exculpatory according to them, or it would have had to be disclosed under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And secondly, none of the underlying witnesses or personnel who provided the information is likely to be a witness before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, under those statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many, 12? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 12. And these statements are being made available in accordance with the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: They haven't been yet, as I understand it, but they will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're now on notice, Mr. Sepenuk, that there's a lot more than 12 available to the Prosecution, it would appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The evidence before the Court since the 89 bis statement is now in evidence that there are 3.000 such forms. But as the Defence knows or should know that the Prosecution has received tens of thousands of forms in relation to refugees. These are forms which indicate what happened and why they left by various organisations that were at the refugee camps. They are available and it really is the responsibility of the Defence to ask for however many of those they want, and we will make them available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, not to beat this to death, the only reason I even mentioned it is that the statement was made that no Defence lawyer had ever requested copies of these documents. It's simply not so. I did at the Status Conference last week. And then, if you don't mind, one other statement. I hate to even bring it up. But when you say there are tens of thousands of these documents available, presumably this report was based on 2700. I don't know whether you spoke advisedly there. But if there are tens of thousands, particularly if in those tens of thousands, if there's anything exculpatory, we would certainly like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to comment too much. Whatever is requested by the Defence will be delivered to them pursuant to the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying there are tens of thousands of forms in relation to refugees? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In relation to refugees. In relation to this report, there are approximately 2700 plus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are you referring to when you say there are tens of thousands of forms?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1999 and 2000 the Prosecution received not only from the KVM mission but from a variety of human rights organisations forms in respect of refugee [indiscernible]. Since we are hearing now that the Defence might want to see the forms in respect of this report, I just want it to be made clear that they must request any of these documents which are in our possession at a reasonable time so that proper arrangements can be made for their delivery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these forms available on the electronic disclosure suite as part of your Kosovo collection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would think not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The documents, I believe, and here I am hardly speculating, were so numerous and they consist primarily of forms, that they were not all scanned into the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all submissions that are -- Mr. O'Sullivan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I must take issue with the position taken by the Prosecution in relation to these statements. He has referred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. O'Sullivan, the decision has been made already that we're going to hear this evidence. And then at the end of all examination, cross-examination, we'll hear the submissions that parties have to make in the light of that. Will that not adequately suffice?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's have Ms. Mitchell back, please. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Ms. Mitchell. Please have a seat again and the examination will continue. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last question I was asking about the report As Seen, As Told. Could you briefly describe, bearing in mind that this is in your statement already, what the report is about and what the sources are for the report.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: The As Seen, As Told report is a culmination of statements received by human rights officers in Kosovo prior to the NATO air campaign. Upon the withdrawal of the mission, information was collected from refugees to continue the human rights mandate of monitoring the situation inside Kosovo. And the second part of the report includes statements and information collected by human rights officers after the NATO air campaign between June and September 1999 during the implementation of the -- a different Security Council resolution and the demilitarisation of the UCK and the withdrawal of the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when was it published?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Both reports were published together in order to provide a complete picture. Given the seriousness of many of the findings, we felt it very important to release both reports at the same time. And they were released in December 1999, when the analysis was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we discuss briefly the methodology in collecting the statements. What was the system used in collecting the statements before the NATO bombing began in March 1999, and what was the system, if there was any change, in collecting these statements after the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Prior to the NATO bombing, as the mission was standing up and as the Court noted, there may have been additional tasks, the human rights division itself was comprised at the time of the withdrawal of about 75 people, but many, many others became involved in the collection of human rights data. And I'll explain that in the methodology. The situation the mission was deployed into was already a critical human rights environment on the ground. There was -- it was a state of marshal law, of military control and occupation of most of the Kosovo Albanian areas. This is a result of the escalation of hostilities over the summer months and then the resulting mandate that I described earlier. Given this critical human rights situation and large-scale displacement of over 2 or 300.000 people, the sheer volume of the information that we were seeing and that the field staff was seeing throughout Kosovo required that we prioritise, as much as possible. So we began prioritising on statements from victims and direct witness accounts. We had a fairly intrusive monitoring mandate under the agreement with Yugoslavia. The mission was not only monitoring the human rights situation but was also monitoring a cease-fire that had been agreed to and the withdrawal of specific numbers of Serbian security forces and their return to barracks. So there was all kinds of monitoring going on at the time, all of which was impacting the lives of people in the communities and their human rights. So to collect this kind of information in such a critical environment with such volumes, we had to go to very centralised, standard reporting. And the operational guidelines, the tasks, instructions of how this was to be done are all attached to my statement. So I won't go into that, except to state that the methodology we used was basically on really two criteria: One was to ensure the highest reliability of the information; and that it be collected in an impartial way. One has to remember that nowhere does any authority admit to human rights violations. Authorities do not cooperate with the investigations of human rights situations, particularly in a state of military conflict that we found ourselves in. So reliability and impartiality became very critical. We felt the only way we could do that, bearing in mind how politicised the conflict in Kosovo had been with Yugoslavia and the international community, staff were recruited that were all -- either had law enforcement background, police officers deployed in contingents from some host countries. We had military officers put into a civilian capacity that were helping with logistics and security. This was armed conflict, so there was a lot of dangerous security situations that staff were being put into. From the human rights perspective, we were very conscious of the fact that information we were collecting about killings that we were seeing was highly sensitive and had to be handled in that way. So the protocols were standardised investigation forms along the types that you would normally see by law enforcement officials. Because of the gravity of what was going on, training for staff in how these forms would be completed. They would be collected weekly in headquarters. Staff were not allowed to keep copies of any of the materials. Their original notes were taken out of their notebooks and attached to statements. As far as investigations, again, the sheer number of the complaints -- when we left Kosovo, we had 750 complaints. These, again, would have been all victim or direct witness accounts of serious crimes, killings, massacres, et cetera. All we could really try to do in those situations was to get additional information, document the crime scenes, get additional statements, corroborate the information, and then closely monitor any official investigations that were going on, and in so doing, was monitoring the administration of justice in the court systems in Kosovo at that time. That information was compiled on a weekly basis, a monthly basis, and spot reports were also issued on specific critical events. And I would describe those as killings of three or more people with strong implications that the security services may have been involved. When the decision was taken to withdraw the KVM from Kosovo on March 20th because of the deteriorating security conditions and the escalation of the violence, additional troops being deployed from Serbia into Kosovo, et cetera, all the human rights information was assembled by five senior human rights officers in their areas of responsibility. Documents that were not relevant to these 750 cases were shredded, burned, destroyed, as was a large part of the administration side of the mission. We assembled that information in Skopje, and it remained in my custody until it was subsequently transferred to the office in Warsaw in June of 1999 for analysis and preparation of the report. The information -- the methodology for collecting refugee statements, when the mission withdrew and we started seeing these huge numbers of people pouring over the borders in Afghan -- in Albania and in Macedonia, we quickly realised that some of the stories we were hearing initially at the borders were just replications of violence that we had already been seeing and that this was going to be a very serious humanitarian situation. So OSCE reconfigured the stand-down of the mission. We evacuated 1300 people within weeks. That number went down to about 450 internationals, 200 of whom were working in the camps in Albania and in Macedonia as their being stood up, perhaps helping first with the humanitarian preparations but quickly others came in to do that. And information was then collected from refugees. And using a standardised form, which I believe is also in my statement, we were -- we asked the same questions of refugees. We again were identifying only victims and direct-witness accounts. The KVM had very, very high credibility with the Albanian population. In any critical human rights environment, people will seek protection. Many Albanians sought protection from the KVM, so in the camps when they saw the bright orange cars of the KVM they would provide us with assistance in identifying the most critical -- most critical evidence, frankly, that's what we were looking for. So we collected -- and we had two processes going on. I had a deputy managing Macedonia. I was in Albania moving back and forth. Every day the statements that were collected in the camps were centralised, and the original copies were provided to the Prosecutor's office, with one copy retained, and again, in my custody or in my deputy's custody, the information was put into databases, particularly the location of where the refugee was from, the gender of the refugee, so that we could ensure that we were getting -- collecting as much information as we could from all the municipalities in Kosovo, as well as ensuring that we were getting a gender balance and not just receiving statements from men, which is the traditional custom for Albanians. That information at the end of the NATO air campaign was far too sensitive to take back into Kosovo, so an agreement was reached with the OSCE office in Warsaw, where I had previously worked before deploying to Kosovo, that we would send all of those files, including the refugee statements and the files that had been evacuated to Warsaw, where they were transported by the Polish military. Chain of custody was ensured through this whole time. Refugee statements were numbered, they were kept in binders. A meant Albania, M meant Macedonia. They were organised by municipality, et cetera. Once in Warsaw, I deployed back into Kosovo and re-started the human rights activities using a similar process to document the revenge and the reprisals, which isn't the topic of this particular proceeding. The information, once in Warsaw, a team of six to eight human rights experts was assembled, including my deputy, who was very familiar, obviously, with the whole operation. And they reviewed the information according to a standardised series of classifications, which is also attached to my statement, which goes into more detail of classification, verifying the information. When -- as this report is -- that hopefully will be before you was prepared, statements were corroborated. We had roughly 2800 statements, 1100 from the Albanian -- from Albania, 1600 collected in the camps in Macedonia. The numbers reflect the more serious humanitarian situation in Albania, which took a lot of the tasking time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before -- could I just clarify a couple of things. The -- if we take the first volume of this report or the first report, as you called it, that deals with 750 complaints, did you say, of serious incidents and -- and they were all prior to the 20th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. And -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then it also deals with refugees' responses. Do they post-date the 20th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how far -- how late do they go in volume 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The refugee monitoring plan, our mandate to do that, was authorised two days after the withdrawal, so from March 22nd. The mission redeployed into Kosovo officially bringing in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where does volume 1 end, though, on what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It ends on June 10th, which is the date that KFOR entered Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you said that you had your own -- you had 75 human rights officers there, but they were supplemented by many others with an interest in human rights. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. When we would have a critical incident, either in Kosovo, for example, Racak, other staff would be pulled in to assist with the documentation from the field operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. So the many others were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within KVM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- OSCE or KVM people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're not just miscellaneous helpers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope not. There was different departments within the KVM, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the second volume you say covers the period from June to September. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what does -- have you covered what it's dealing with so far, or were you confining your remarks so far to the first volume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've confined my remarks to the first volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Since you're on the second volume and since objectivity is an issue which we would like to discuss, what was the second volume about, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: The redeployment back into Kosovo saw a shrinking of the human rights division from several hundred in the camps back down to 75 was restarted in the five regional areas and documented acts of violence and crimes being committed against the remaining minority population in Kosovo, which consisted of Kosovo Serbs, Roma, Askali, Turks, Bosniaks, et cetera, often referred to as the period of revenge and reprisals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, the two reports for the relevant period covered and reported upon human rights violations committed against every ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to comment briefly on the human rights division operational plan which was referred to in your statement. Perhaps it could be brought up. It's P763. And I do this with some trepidation, having worked with e-court system before. The human rights division operational plan of December 1990, was this the basic guidelines that your staff operated under and was it transmitted to all your staff?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at page 3 of it. And I have been told that I am -- page 3 on the B/C/S version accords with page 3 on the English version. Could we scroll down a little, please. Could we scroll down so I could see all of the paragraph 2.3? Could you scroll up so I could just see paragraph 2.3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these guidelines the OSCE -- and I read now: "The OSCE must strive for impartiality in the area of human rights. Impartiality connotes fairness and justice, and what is to be strived for is absolute objectivity, not unquestioned inaction. The OSCE must not freeze into inaction through a fear of upsetting some, or at times all, of the parties to the conflict. The aggrieved party views silence as passive complicity and partiality. The violators see it as passive acceptance or symbol of OSCE weakness." And at the end of this section, the operational principle: "KVM action in promoting and protecting human rights will be even-handed and consistent so as to be impartial and neutral." Can you comment on that? Is that the functioning guideline for your staff on the collection of the statements which form the basis of the report?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. And it was a huge portion of the psyche within the human rights department that we be seen to be impartial and independent because we were operating in a highly political environment and a mission that was managing military relations, et cetera. So we -- our division had independence from many of the other departments as far as not having to share information. We -- I reported directly to the head of mission, and we had our freedom to pursue investigations without consultation with any of the political leaders to ensure our independence. So this -- these paragraphs that you're referring to on impartiality were extremely important in the conduct of all the people working in the human rights of the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this same document, could we proceed to page 13? Again, I've been told that the -- it is the same page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned training of staff and the importance it was in your mission to have not only adequate staff but staff who were adequately trained. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we scroll to paragraph 5.3 of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it correct that the KVM, as indicated in your statement in evidence, recognised the complexity of the monitoring situation you were in and made adequate arrangements for the training and induction of competent staff for the collection of these statements?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. The staff were often active police officers in OSCE countries that were immediately seconded to the mission, several hundred, as well as logistical support, IT support. Training was done in Brezovica, which is an area outside of Pristina, that received -- everybody going into the KVM went through several days of induction training. They received information on human rights as well as other aspects of the mission's mandate. And then within the human rights division as staff were assigned, we gave them additional training on the use of forms. We didn't have to do too much training on the technical side because most people had human rights experience, policing experience, and had, in fact, worked in conflict situations before. So it was more adapting them to the needs of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we scroll down a little, although I think your answer covers the section that I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's covered. In this document you -- in the annexes to the document, which is a significant part of the document, if not about half, therein you make provisions for additional training of the staff because of the complexity of the situation there.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Regrettably we weren't in Kosovo long enough to do all of the tasks that were given to us. So the initial trainings focussed on trial monitoring because the administration of justice prior to the evacuation was being used to further violate the human rights of the majority of the population, as well as documenting critical humanitarian law situations, managing issues of dead bodies, killings, things of this nature, and those were the initial trainings that were focussed on. We evacuated too soon before other things could get put into place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at page 5, that's paragraphs 3 and 3.1 at page 5 of that report, of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You ensured in your training procedures, it is the evidence in your statement, that your staff or the staff responsible for collecting these statements were made well acquainted, if they had not been acquainted before, with the international humanitarian law norms and standards?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct. Every staff member received a binder when they reported to our office for assignment after going through Brezovica, and they got a copy of the operational plan, the mandate, the different mandates we discussed earlier today, all of those original documents, as well as tips and how to complete reports, a full manual was given to every staff member and they read them and we had weekly meetings to ensure that everybody was on top of things. It was a very fast-moving environment. A lot of violence going on. The staff were highly motivated and highly compliant with the procedures in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you scroll down that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we see there some of the international humanitarian and human rights law instruments there indicated.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you say that your mandate arose out of the United Nations resolution and the agreement signed between the FRY and the OSCE. But speaking from your own perspective as a lawyer, lawyer involved in human rights, what ultimately was the purpose of that report, that assimilation of information from the refugees and the preparation of the report?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: There was very little we could do to stop the violations from occurring at the time we were there. All I felt we could really do was to do the best job we could in documenting and bearing witness. This was a very large peacekeeping operation. Kosovo is a fairly small place of less than 2 million people. You can drive from one end to the other in a few hours. 1300 people is a lot. We wanted to document, we wanted to bear witness, and we wanted to do it in a way that provided reliable and impartial information for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, just before I move on, just a few mop-up questions. The second report that you did in respect to the allegations of atrocities committed against Serbs and other non-Kosovar Albanian ethnicities, did you use the same methodology?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, we used the same methodology. Some of the output looks a little different because the second report was prepared in-country while we had other tasks going on and we didn't have the volume of information. The second report is of a more focussed area, as you say, just focussing on really the minority situation and certainly the scale of the violations reported in both reports is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to Kosovo in June 1999, as your statement indicates, there was some follow-up investigations, and you of course had had the opportunity to make observations from the field. Now, were there any observations from the field upon your return to Kosovo in 1999 that would cause you or that were inconsistent with the conclusions of the report in As Seen, As Told, Part I, or do they confirm the report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, a bit of a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's in her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, that is right, but I'm observing. Just to indicate that's the -- it's examination-in-chief. I'm sorry for this, but -- I know it's difficult, all that is too big. But yet we are to observe the rules of evidence. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you returned to Kosovo in June 1999, did your observations in any way impact on the conclusions that you made in respect to As Seen, As Told, Part I?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Again, there was no way that we could follow up on all the refugees statements that were collected. The volume was too great, and the situation was still very difficult in Kosovo for the minorities during those months. We saw absolutely nothing but substantiation of the statements that we received from the refugees and their conclusions. And our priority was to try to assist in the identification of where graves were that we had heard from in the refugee statements. So we went back into Kosovo with a list of sites and quickly deployed teams first to those sites to try to secure them for future investigation by the Prosecutor's office, which was standing up at the same time. And the sites that were visited are contained in an annex in the second report because they were done during that phase of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said it was published in December 1999. Let's just discuss briefly what you mean by publish. Was it publicly disseminated and to what extent was it?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was a much-anticipated series of reports. There was high anxiety and expectations about what impact these reports could have. The OSCE had never undertaken such a thing before. A human rights operation had never been able to work and contribute so much during the crimes as they were being committed. The reports were released in Pristina, in Vienna, in Warsaw, in Belgrade all at the same time. Press conferences were conducted, and the findings of these reports were on the front page of the New York Times, the Washington Post, BBC, most European newspapers that weekend. Official copies of the report were delivered to all delegations of the OSCE, including the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and was given to their official representatives in Belgrade as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a very long report, so -- and we can't cover all the details here. Could you just tell us briefly, in our own words, what were the primary conclusions of the report. For example, let's start with the primary reasons for the refugees' departure from Kosovo between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, I am going to object to that, Your Honour. The -- that's a conclusion for this Trial Chamber to make. I don't think it's an appropriate question for this witness. That's -- she's not qualified as an expert witness, and that's for the Chamber to conclude. That's, indeed, one of the pivotal issues in this case. And for this witness to be expressing her own opinion on that, Your Honour, I really believe is quite improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness testified about conclusions drawn from the report prepared on the basis of a mandate given to the Kosovo Verification Mission by a United Nations resolution. She's entitled to comment on the work product done under, her testimony, her supervision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But as a matter of fact, if you introduce the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: -- and she will read the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But once she start commenting on the report, then it becomes -- if the comments are already in the report, why should we take an aversion then? I would say that -- introduce the report. That's the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. It's one of the questions here because much of it is covered in her 89(F) statement. We have to draw a sort of balance between try to save time by the use of 89(F) and also public trials. So although the information is in the report, I ask her to summarise some areas of the report just for the purposes of putting on the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- following the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise for interfering. The report is already -- will be on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Once it is on record, we will read it; it becomes a public document. However, you can suggest to her -- if I were there I would say: Have you anything else to add? Finished. And let her add but not that you suggest to her to comment and the comments are already in the report itself. That would make a little -- I mean, it's -- can't be received like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: It can't be received like that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have anything else to say, on this Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What if I put the question thus -- this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the statements you received, did you receive from the on-the-line persons interviewed, any information as to why they left Kosovo in that period and is that reported in As Seen, As Told?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. The motivations for why the refugees left Kosovo is discussed in detail in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to the reasons given these by persons, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll object again, Your Honour. He's trying to get, I hate to use this cliche, through the backdoor. He is trying to get a conclusion from this witness that I think is an improper conclusion for her to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what's your response to that? It's the same question by a different route.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it -- the question -- I'm not sure if I got a ruling in respect to the admissibility of the answer. It is my submission that she is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean you're not sure if you got a ruling? You carried on -- you withdrew the question and asked another one. So the Court wasn't asked to rule. You didn't insist, so you're now facing another objection, and I'm looking for your response to that other objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, which I'm -- again, the response is the same. The witness is testifying about a -- the product of her work, work done under her supervision, that was done as a result of a mandate given to her on the United Nations resolution and an agreement between the FRY and the KVM. She -- it is my submission she is, therefore, entitled to comment on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, internationally it is known that when something is given in the form of a document, then the document speaks. If there's anything to be argumented which is missing from the document, that has another aspect. But here is a document, is being produced, let her do it. But opinion from the witness, how will that come in this particular case, when she has formally reported and we are taking the report. How will she orally say something beyond that unless there is something missing, which, for coherence, she has to put in. It's just to put it across so that we get wiser by your comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the Trial Chamber is not prepared to allow this question because it carries with it the danger of the expression of a personal opinion by the witness. And the report has already been tendered for our consideration in the context of this evidence as a whole. And on the basis of the report, we will reach a conclusion ultimately on whether it should be admitted and, if so, to what extent it should be admitted. So the question is going to add nothing to our knowledge of the overall circumstances, and in these circumstances we invite you to proceed with another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. That was, in fact, the last area I wanted to cover in chief. As I indicated before, most of the evidence in chief is reflected in the 89 bis package. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before the cross-examination proceeds, may I make an inquiry as to what the procedure should be. Do we -- should I tender now or should I wait until the end of the cross-examination? There are different practices in different courts. I think that Your Honour ruled that in respect to As Seen, As Told we should wait until we hear the evidence in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- other documents she referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All the documents in this case in relation to this witness's evidence will be considered by the Chamber. They're available to us on the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All you need to do is tell us the numbers of all the documents you wish us to read, or consider at least, and we'll consider them. So far as tendering them so that they may be formally admitted, then that can't be done until we have actually -- well, we know that you're tendering them and we will make our ruling under admissibility in due course. You don't need to do any more at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll proceed in the order of the indictment for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We've heard that you were the director of the human rights division of OSCE for the period of April -- sorry, October 1998 to April 2000?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But before the mission was underway -- before the KVM mission got started in October or thereabouts, 1998, you were a legal advisor to OSCE?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were -- participated in the planning and deployment of this mission?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Another member of the KVM mission who testified in the Milosevic case estimated that by February of 1999 there were approximately 1.600 people in your mission. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sounds a little high. I think it would have been closer to about 1300, but it depends if you count the national staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this witness estimated that approximately half of those people were filling what he called administrative functions, office work, clerk work, not going into the field. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think it would be more like 30 per cent were probably supporting the field activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. So of the 70 per cent who went into the field, that -- that number of people -- that would have been a difficult task to collect data and it would have hampered the performance of the KVM, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: For a hundred per cent to be deployed?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, for 70 per cent of the --

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, that's about average.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the person I'm referring to, and I want to put this to you, who testified in the Milosevic trial as a man by the name of Roland Keith who had spent 32 years in the Canadian military, and he was assigned as a verifier. And he had this to say in his evidence. He said: "I would hazard a guess that only half of us were sent to the field. The other half were doing headquarters-type work, administrative work, and directional work, but our ability, and I stress this very, very strongly, our inability to monitor the KVM at the field level was apparent to me from day one." Now, is there any reason why we shouldn't accept what Mr. Keith said about his work in the field?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's Mr. Keith's opinion. I do not agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, were you in the field?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And what was the difference between what Mr. Keith has to say?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I don't know what department Mr. Keith was in. People were assigned to different departments at different times. There were hundreds of people going in and out of taskings, moving around to cover hot spots. It was a very robust field operation with more than 40 field locations established. So I think it was intensively covering the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think in one of your statements you described, and I think you've said it here as well, that it was a fast-moving mission and there were logistical challenges for all staff. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a question about the training -- or the initial training the verifiers got. And I think it was probably -- it's fair to say having looked through your statement that a lot of the verifiers got what you called on-the-job training?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that on-the-job training is sporadic and haphazard?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, I would not, because these individuals came with the skill set necessary to adapt very quickly. Many of them had law enforcement, military, human rights backgrounds working in conflict situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness can be shown P763, please. Page 22 of that exhibit, please. And please bear with me because I want to go down -- would the ERN help you? I'm asking the court officer. The ERN is K0227483. That's the page I want within that document. 7483.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm told that is page 22, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, then it must be the annex to it. Is there an an -- perhaps the Prosecution can assist, but I'm looking for the draft annex 1 to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's the right document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page of that document and scroll down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think he wants to go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Second page. Okay. And scroll down a bit, just a little more, little more, little more. All right. The second full paragraph, it says: "In addition, the relatively short tour of duty of most KVM members (six months for many) makes it essential that training occur quickly and is not left to the haphazard and often slow dynamics of the on-the-job training." And I put it to you that your document recognises that the on-the-job training is haphazard.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, most of the verifiers received on-the-job training. You've told us that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I believe I also said that most verifiers came with the skill set necessary to rapidly adapt to the situation and the training they received was how to fulfil the procedures, the mandate of the KVM, and that portion it was, yes, mostly on the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you said some of them but not all of them did, come with the skills and the training. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Most of them. I mean, it was a minority that were not in position. And usually we transferred them to other departments. Sort of the normal personnel management issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you said some of the trained persons were, in fact, former police officers, military people, that sort of person, right?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: And human rights people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the ones with experience, you would agree, would be in a position to evaluate perhaps those that were not experienced and properly trained. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Assuming they knew the context in which to make the evaluation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'd like to read a short passage, Your Honour, to the witness. This is Mr. Keith speaking, the man who spent 32 years in the Canadian military. He was asked by the Presiding Judge, Judge Robinson, whether verifiers were sent out into the field with a training programme, and he was asked whether he could answer that question. And Mr. Keith said this: "Yes, I can, Your Honour, and I would be pleased to. Upon arrival it was mostly administrative and technical training, the competency to handle a Peugeot four-wheel drive sport utility vehicle competently on the roads of Kosovo was taken. I must say it was pretty rudimentary, but everyone did have to pass a test. The ability to operate a radio was provided. The ability to use a GPS, global positioning sensor, and some of the briefings of what was taking place in the province by various high officials from within the mission was provided to people to try to give some sense of what the situation was in the province. And course, to a very limited degree, if I may, direction on what to do. But in my humble opinion, and Mr. Nice in questioning my credibility due to my limited rank -- rise in rank, in my humble opinion, it was very rudimentary and at no time was anybody given, and certainly I wasn't, information of what we were looking at, what we may be looking out. No booklets were given to and were accessible to people of what the organisation of the VJ was and the organisation of the MUP was, but my -- Mr. Nice referred to Staff College, staff training. This was -- this was certainly not a staff document." Then Judge Robinson asks: "Was there any training in identifying the matters that ought to be reported on? "A. No, Your Honour, I could honestly say other than: Report what you see." Now, is there any reason to question and not accept what Mr. Keith said?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have a transcript page number for that reference, and for the earlier one I think?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. My apology for not saying that at the outset. This last portion is -- begins on page 32800 and continues on to the next page, 32801. And the first passage is page 32825, both on the Milosevic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can I ask you what Mr. Keith 's particular duties were in the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, he -- he led -- he led a small -- or a mission. He was a verifier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the witness has been dealing with human rights -- people who are checking on human rights violations. There were verifiers doing other things, for example, movement -- troop movements and so on. Do we know what his responsibility was? We know he was military, and therefore it may be that he was involved in something other than human rights observations. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll have to check that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just ask in addition to that if we could have the date of the testimony. We are trying to find it, but I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The 14th of September, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But the training that Mr. Keith described is no greater than verifiers receive, is it?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I would describe those more as briefings on the communication and security protocols in place for the mission, which included ensuring that people knew how to manage the vehicles, the equipment, things of this nature. It's very standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But the inexperienced people, whether they're looking at military movements or alleged human rights abuses, if you're not trained in looking at what you're seeing, there's no way of knowing exactly how to interpret what you're seeing. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think the question's a little confusing, if I may say, because we were there to bear witness and to report and to verify allegations. One needs a skill set of proper -- knowing how to do proper documentation, how to record things in an impartial and reliable way; and for those purposes, the staffs did have the skill set plus the additional experience of working in a highly volatile and insecure physical environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in that environment your ability to move around was quite limited, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: It would depend. We had movement, for the most part, around Kosovo. When incidents were occurring, then the VJ and the Serbian security forces would prevent us from entering into those areas. So freedom of movement was very much a day-to-day, incident-to-incident, zone-to-zone type of environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So is it your position here today that your movement was not restricted the whole time you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I believe I just answered that question, that for the most part we had movement on the main roads. There were check-points. We observed the check-points. We often had to negotiate access through the check-points. There were situations where, yes, we were denied access by the security forces to incidents. So I would say that freedom of movement was as challenging in the Kosovo armed conflict situation as it is in any situation like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that for a moment. But your movements were restricted to main roads. You didn't go off the beaten tracks?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Oh, that's not true. No, we did go off the beaten tracks. We tried to get access to very remote locations and villages. Many of the roads in Kosovo are dirt roads, at least at time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you tried and did not succeed?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Case by case.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you said that -- you testified -- you testified in the Milosevic trial. You said that during the war, when you were in Albania and Macedonia, you had a total of 200 staff members, including interpreters and locals. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, if we had the transcript page and date.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Fine. It's page 7545.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll read -- in fact, I'll just read what you said in the Milosevic trial, page 7545. "Well, we had at full strength 200 staff members dispersed in Albania and in Macedonia that included our national colleagues, interpreters, et cetera. 75 of those staff were deployed in Albania, which was under a horrendous humanitarian catastrophe because of the influx of so many refugees that came in what seemed to be controlled spurts of 50.000 a day for a few days, et cetera. So the 200 working a day is a little deceptive. The mission was going through a phase-down at the time, so it took a little while to get organised." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila, do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have several questions, but it's quite late in the day and we only have five minutes to go. I'm not sure if I should start now. I certainly can if you want me to. There's no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought we would get more value for money in five minutes from you than from anyone else, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] That's fine, that's fine. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Fila. Let's hear the beginning of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Mitchell, I read your statement. It says that you're in charge of systematic gathering of data on human rights violations. At first you were there -- you were there throughout, but the first period before people started leaving Kosovo. When you say "human rights violations," that applies equally to all ethnic groups, doesn't it, or at least that's what -- when I say "human rights violations," you take that to include all the ethnic groups there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In this first period and up to the 20th of March, that's what we're talking about, which is when you left Kosovo, you withdrew. What I want to know is after the 20th of March, was there a TV appearance for you in Montenegro or not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a mission in Montenegro, because some of the refugees went to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: The mandate for our particular operation that I've described today did not extend to Montenegro, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me rephrase this. Before you arrived there, did your mission entail any sort of training in terms of the historical background for Kosovo and Metohija; for example, did you study the various reasons for various cases where exodus occurred in Kosovo throughout the 19th and 20th century? Did you study the reasons behind these? Did you know about all of these or was that simply not part of your background training?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I had worked in the Balkans for more than ten years and I was aware of the history, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's precisely the reason I'm asking because you did say that at the outset, didn't you. I wanted to lead you up to that again. What about that situation in Kosovo that you found when you came there? Was this something that only started then, whereas earlier on everything used to be all right, or is there a whole history behind this of trends and even growing hatred? The suffering, the casualties, the hatred, all the different cases where there was an exodus, before you came there, that's what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a little unclear how to answer the question, but yes, this was a deteriorating security situation that began in full earnest as far back as 1989 and only got worse. I don't know how far back you want me to go in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As far back as you can; that's how far I want you to go. In terms of your knowledge, you referred to the last ten years, the ten years before your arrival, was everything fine in Kosovo in those ten years? Because what comes across is that everything began in 1999 or back in 1990 and up to that point everything was just pure gravy. Do you know the history of this entire evolving trend, if I may call it that, throughout the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could help me, Mr. Fila, with the relevance of that question and the relevance of the witness's knowledge of the -- the whole developing trend throughout the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The relevance is I believe we have to establish whether the whole thing came about, the lack of trust, the exodus, everything that occurred in 1998, which is what the indictment suggests, or were there cases that were familiar from before but only escalating now? Because there's no logic in that. The joint criminal enterprise would imply that up to 1998 everybody lived in general happiness, and then suddenly something erupted between these people that marred their relations. That's not how it was, so that's what I'm trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand entirely the point that you're trying to make, and there may be -- it may be appropriate, to some extent, to explore historical and political contexts in this trial. But this witness is dealing with whether or not there were human rights violations, and it seems to me that history and political background don't have a lot to do with the question: Was this particular conduct a violation of human rights? Was it an atrocity? Was it a behaviour that was criminal? So I doubt very much if exploring her background knowledge of the Balkan history is actually relevant to the evidence she's giving. Now, on that note, we will adjourn. You can think about how you might approach the matter in light of that expression of view, and we will resume the case tomorrow at 2.15, when your cross-examination of Ms. Mitchell will continue. You know the routine by now, Ms. Mitchell, since we've heard that you've been here before, and no doubt had your evidence interrupted before, that you shouldn't be in discussion with anybody overnight about the evidence that you're giving here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll see you tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of July, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.00 p.m.,
